# Chapter 94: Writing Task 1 Overview

**Part:** 6 — IELTS Writing


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## What Academic Task 1 assesses
In Academic Writing Task 1, you write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes to describe a graph, chart, table, map, or process. The task measures four public criteria: Task Achievement, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. It is not a test of your opinion. A report that explains reasons not shown in the visual can become less relevant even when its English is fluent.

## The core method: read, select, organise, verify
First, read the rubric and visual with forensic care. Identify the unit, time period, and categories. Second, select the dominant features: extremes, major changes, stable items, intersections, and striking contrasts. Third, organise related information rather than following a visual mechanically. Finally, verify that every figure, tense, and comparison is accurate.

## Structure that serves the reader
Use an introduction to paraphrase, a separate overview to communicate the main patterns, and two focused detail paragraphs. The overview is indispensable: it answers “what should a busy reader notice first?” A line graph may require trends; a bar chart may require rankings; a map may require the principal redevelopments; a process may require its start, finish, and linear or cyclical nature.

## Timing and language
Spend roughly three minutes planning, fourteen minutes drafting, and three minutes checking. Use precise reporting verbs: *stood at, accounted for, rose to, fell by, exceeded, remained stable*. Use comparison grammar: *while, whereas, compared with, respectively, twice as high as*. Do not manufacture complexity. One accurate complex sentence is better than three unstable ones.

## Error patterns
Do not omit the overview; list every number; use a conclusion that repeats it; report causes not supplied; confuse *rise to* with *rise by*; or describe a future projection as a past fact. Keep the report objective: “The figure increased” rather than “I think the figure increased.”

## Practice protocol
Collect ten authentic-style visuals. For each, make a 90-second plan, write an overview without numbers, and select six supporting data points. Then write under timed conditions. Review with a four-colour code: one colour for overview claims, one for figures, one for comparisons, and one for errors. If a body paragraph contains figures but no comparison, rewrite it.

## Mini model
The line graph compares annual visits to two museums from 2010 to 2020. Overall, attendance at the modern-art museum rose substantially, whereas visits to the history museum were broadly stable. Starting at 120,000, the former climbed to nearly 250,000 before easing slightly. The latter fluctuated between 140,000 and 155,000, so the initially smaller venue became the more popular one by the middle of the period.

## Final checklist
Have you met the word minimum; accurately paraphrased; supplied a real overview; grouped evidence; used the right tense; checked plurals, articles, spelling, and units; and avoided personal opinion? These habits make a report reliable at every band.

### Timed refinement drill 1: identify the central comparison before writing
In a Academic Task 1 response response, spend two minutes on this controlled exercise. Write one overview sentence that names the largest contrast, then test whether every detail paragraph supports it.
Draft two sentences, read them aloud once, and revise only errors you can name. This is deliberate practice: accuracy comes before speed. Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. On the next attempt, use a new data point or idea so that you practise transfer rather than memorisation.

# Chapter 95: Line Graphs

**Part:** 6 — IELTS Writing Task 1 (Academic)


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Purpose and success criteria
Line graphs require you to describe change, rate, direction, turning points, and relative position over time. These tasks test your ability to select, organise, and compare visual information in at least 150 words. They do not reward specialist knowledge or imaginative explanation. A strong report gives a faithful overview, groups related features, and supports each comparison with accurate data. Aim to plan for three minutes, write for fourteen, and reserve three minutes to check units, tense, articles, and spelling.

## Reliable four-paragraph structure
1. **Introduction:** paraphrase the task in one sentence: chart type, subject, place, and period.
2. **Overview:** state two or three highest-level features. Do not load this paragraph with every number.
3. **Body paragraph 1:** present a logical group, usually the largest values, a shared trend, or the first time period.
4. **Body paragraph 2:** complete the remaining meaningful comparison.

The structure is not a formula for copying. Its purpose is to make the reader see your organisation. If a graphic has two strongly contrasting groups, compare them by group; if it has a clear chronology, compare it by stage.

## How to analyse before writing
Read the title, axes, legend, units, dates, and footnotes. Ask: What is measured? Which feature is highest or lowest? What changes most? Where do categories converge, diverge, overtake, or remain stable? Circle no more than six useful figures. An overview is a judgement about patterns, not a shortened data dump.

For a typical prompt, imagine that a city’s bicycle use rises from 20 to 45 thousand journeys while bus use stays close to 30 thousand. Your notes might be: “first measure rises strongly; second remains near 30; widest gap in middle; first still leads at end.” These notes can become an overview. Exact figures belong in the body paragraphs.

## Vocabulary with control
Use words only when their meanings match the evidence.

**Upward:** climb, rise, grow, surge, recover, reach a peak. **Downward:** decline, dip, drop, plunge, bottom out. **No major change:** level off, plateau, remain stable, fluctuate within a narrow range. **Nouns:** an increase, a decline, a fluctuation, a peak, a trough.

For movement, use a verb plus an optional adverb: *rose gradually, fell sharply, remained broadly stable*. For a static comparison, prefer *stood at, accounted for, was twice as high as, exceeded, lagged behind*. Avoid “dramatically” for a change of one unit and avoid “respectively” unless the order is unmistakable.

## Sentence patterns
- X **stood at** 24%, compared with 18% for Y.
- X **rose from** 20 **to** 45, an increase of 25 units.
- While X increased, Y **remained broadly unchanged**.
- At 60%, A was **three times the proportion of** B.
- After peaking at 45, the figure **edged down** to 42.

Use past tense for completed periods, present tense for a chart with no time reference, and future language only for projections. Do not write “increased by 45” when the value rose *to* 45; that confuses change with final level.

## Common mistakes and repairs
**Listing:** “A was 20. B was 30. C was 40.” Repair it with a comparison: “A and B were lower than C, at 20 and 30 versus 40.”

**Missing overview:** A report can contain accurate details yet lose Task Achievement marks. Write the overview immediately after the introduction.

**Inventing explanations:** “This happened because people preferred…” is speculation. Report the visual, not an imagined cause.

**Mechanical grouping:** Chronological order is not always logical. Group values when that makes a trend clearer.

**Inaccurate approximation:** Use *about, roughly,* or *just over* only when the visual does not support precision. Never alter a clearly labelled number.

## Practice tasks
1. Write a 20-minute report on a graphic in which one category rises from 12% to 48%, two categories remain near 25%, and another falls from 35% to 18%.
2. Create an overview using no numbers for a chart with six categories. Then select five figures that prove it.
3. Rewrite a 170-word report that has no comparisons. Add contrast language without changing the facts.
4. Exchange a report with a partner and check every number against the source.

## Self-assessment checklist
Before submitting, ask: Have I described the visual rather than explained it? Is there a separate overview? Does each body paragraph have a grouping principle? Are all units and comparisons accurate? Have I used a range of precise language naturally? Are there at least 150 words, with no irrelevant conclusion?

### Band 6 sample answer
The graphic shows that a city’s bicycle use rises from 20 to 45 thousand journeys while bus use stays close to 30 thousand. Overall, there was a clear difference between the main categories. The first measure was generally higher, although the pattern changed near the end. In the first period, the leading figure rose from 20 to 45, while the other value stayed close to 30. It then fell slightly. By the final period, the gap had become smaller. This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.

**Why it earns this level:** This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.
### Band 7 sample answer
The graphic shows that a city’s bicycle use rises from 20 to 45 thousand journeys while bus use stays close to 30 thousand. Overall, the dominant category increased and finished first, whereas the smaller category was comparatively stable. At the outset, the two measures were 20 and 30 respectively. The leading series then climbed to 45 before easing marginally, while its counterpart remained around 30. Consequently, the difference was widest in the middle of the period. The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.

**Why it earns this level:** The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.
### Band 8 sample answer
The graphic shows that a city’s bicycle use rises from 20 to 45 thousand journeys while bus use stays close to 30 thousand. Overall, one measure rose markedly to become the clear leader, while the other changed little; the most notable feature was the temporary widening of the gap. Beginning at 20, the first figure more than doubled to 45 before levelling off just below that point. By contrast, the second hovered at approximately 30 throughout. Thus, the series diverged sharply mid-period and remained separated at the close. The response groups information and uses data accurately.

**Why it earns this level:** The response groups information and uses data accurately.
### Band 9 sample answer
The graphic shows that a city’s bicycle use rises from 20 to 45 thousand journeys while bus use stays close to 30 thousand. Overall, the principal measure expanded substantially, whereas the comparator was virtually static, producing a pronounced and enduring disparity after the midpoint. From a relatively modest base of 20, the former accelerated to 45, then consolidated at a marginally lower level. The latter, however, fluctuated only within a narrow band around 30. # Chapter 96: Bar Charts

**Part:** 6 — IELTS Writing Task 1 (Academic)


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Purpose and success criteria
Bar charts usually require clear comparison between discrete categories, places, or years. These tasks test your ability to select, organise, and compare visual information in at least 150 words. They do not reward specialist knowledge or imaginative explanation. A strong report gives a faithful overview, groups related features, and supports each comparison with accurate data. Aim to plan for three minutes, write for fourteen, and reserve three minutes to check units, tense, articles, and spelling.

## Reliable four-paragraph structure
1. **Introduction:** paraphrase the task in one sentence: chart type, subject, place, and period.
2. **Overview:** state two or three highest-level features. Do not load this paragraph with every number.
3. **Body paragraph 1:** present a logical group, usually the largest values, a shared trend, or the first time period.
4. **Body paragraph 2:** complete the remaining meaningful comparison.

The structure is not a formula for copying. Its purpose is to make the reader see your organisation. If a graphic has two strongly contrasting groups, compare them by group; if it has a clear chronology, compare it by stage.

## How to analyse before writing
Read the title, axes, legend, units, dates, and footnotes. Ask: What is measured? Which feature is highest or lowest? What changes most? Where do categories converge, diverge, overtake, or remain stable? Circle no more than six useful figures. An overview is a judgement about patterns, not a shortened data dump.

For a typical prompt, imagine that five age groups are compared for weekly exercise, with the 18–29 group leading and the oldest group lowest. Your notes might be: “first measure rises strongly; second remains near 30; widest gap in middle; first still leads at end.” These notes can become an overview. Exact figures belong in the body paragraphs.

## Vocabulary with control
Use words only when their meanings match the evidence.

**Comparisons:** exceed, outstrip, trail, be marginally higher than, be twice the figure for. **Ranking:** lead, rank first, occupy the lowest position. **Values:** stand at, record, register, account for.

For movement, use a verb plus an optional adverb: *rose gradually, fell sharply, remained broadly stable*. For a static comparison, prefer *stood at, accounted for, was twice as high as, exceeded, lagged behind*. Avoid “dramatically” for a change of one unit and avoid “respectively” unless the order is unmistakable.

## Sentence patterns
- X **stood at** 24%, compared with 18% for Y.
- X **rose from** 20 **to** 45, an increase of 25 units.
- While X increased, Y **remained broadly unchanged**.
- At 60%, A was **three times the proportion of** B.
- After peaking at 45, the figure **edged down** to 42.

Use past tense for completed periods, present tense for a chart with no time reference, and future language only for projections. Do not write “increased by 45” when the value rose *to* 45; that confuses change with final level.

## Common mistakes and repairs
**Listing:** “A was 20. B was 30. C was 40.” Repair it with a comparison: “A and B were lower than C, at 20 and 30 versus 40.”

**Missing overview:** A report can contain accurate details yet lose Task Achievement marks. Write the overview immediately after the introduction.

**Inventing explanations:** “This happened because people preferred…” is speculation. Report the visual, not an imagined cause.

**Mechanical grouping:** Chronological order is not always logical. Group values when that makes a trend clearer.

**Inaccurate approximation:** Use *about, roughly,* or *just over* only when the visual does not support precision. Never alter a clearly labelled number.

## Practice tasks
1. Write a 20-minute report on a graphic in which one category rises from 12% to 48%, two categories remain near 25%, and another falls from 35% to 18%.
2. Create an overview using no numbers for a chart with six categories. Then select five figures that prove it.
3. Rewrite a 170-word report that has no comparisons. Add contrast language without changing the facts.
4. Exchange a report with a partner and check every number against the source.

## Self-assessment checklist
Before submitting, ask: Have I described the visual rather than explained it? Is there a separate overview? Does each body paragraph have a grouping principle? Are all units and comparisons accurate? Have I used a range of precise language naturally? Are there at least 150 words, with no irrelevant conclusion?

### Band 6 sample answer
The graphic shows that five age groups are compared for weekly exercise, with the 18–29 group leading and the oldest group lowest. Overall, there was a clear difference between the main categories. The first measure was generally higher, although the pattern changed near the end. In the first period, the leading figure rose from 20 to 45, while the other value stayed close to 30. It then fell slightly. By the final period, the gap had become smaller. This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.

**Why it earns this level:** This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.
### Band 7 sample answer
The graphic shows that five age groups are compared for weekly exercise, with the 18–29 group leading and the oldest group lowest. Overall, the dominant category increased and finished first, whereas the smaller category was comparatively stable. At the outset, the two measures were 20 and 30 respectively. The leading series then climbed to 45 before easing marginally, while its counterpart remained around 30. Consequently, the difference was widest in the middle of the period. The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.

**Why it earns this level:** The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.
### Band 8 sample answer
The graphic shows that five age groups are compared for weekly exercise, with the 18–29 group leading and the oldest group lowest. Overall, one measure rose markedly to become the clear leader, while the other changed little; the most notable feature was the temporary widening of the gap. Beginning at 20, the first figure more than doubled to 45 before levelling off just below that point. By contrast, the second hovered at approximately 30 throughout. Thus, the series diverged sharply mid-period and remained separated at the close. The response groups information and uses data accurately.

**Why it earns this level:** The response groups information and uses data accurately.

## Examiner perspective

The decisive change is not ornate vocabulary; it is better decisions about what matters.

# Chapter 98: Tables

**Part:** 6 — IELTS Writing Task 1 (Academic)


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Purpose and success criteria
Tables contain many values, so selection and meaningful grouping matter more than reporting every cell. These tasks test your ability to select, organise, and compare visual information in at least 150 words. They do not reward specialist knowledge or imaginative explanation. A strong report gives a faithful overview, groups related features, and supports each comparison with accurate data. Aim to plan for three minutes, write for fourteen, and reserve three minutes to check units, tense, articles, and spelling.

## Reliable four-paragraph structure
1. **Introduction:** paraphrase the task in one sentence: chart type, subject, place, and period.
2. **Overview:** state two or three highest-level features. Do not load this paragraph with every number.
3. **Body paragraph 1:** present a logical group, usually the largest values, a shared trend, or the first time period.
4. **Body paragraph 2:** complete the remaining meaningful comparison.

The structure is not a formula for copying. Its purpose is to make the reader see your organisation. If a graphic has two strongly contrasting groups, compare them by group; if it has a clear chronology, compare it by stage.

## How to analyse before writing
Read the title, axes, legend, units, dates, and footnotes. Ask: What is measured? Which feature is highest or lowest? What changes most? Where do categories converge, diverge, overtake, or remain stable? Circle no more than six useful figures. An overview is a judgement about patterns, not a shortened data dump.

For a typical prompt, imagine that four countries are shown for income, electricity use, and life expectancy, with one country leading on all three measures. Your notes might be: “first measure rises strongly; second remains near 30; widest gap in middle; first still leads at end.” These notes can become an overview. Exact figures belong in the body paragraphs.

## Vocabulary with control
Use words only when their meanings match the evidence.

**Table language:** respectively, in contrast, by comparison, the corresponding figure, the former/latter, a gap of. **Quantities:** approximately, precisely, just over, nearly, on average.

For movement, use a verb plus an optional adverb: *rose gradually, fell sharply, remained broadly stable*. For a static comparison, prefer *stood at, accounted for, was twice as high as, exceeded, lagged behind*. Avoid “dramatically” for a change of one unit and avoid “respectively” unless the order is unmistakable.

## Sentence patterns
- X **stood at** 24%, compared with 18% for Y.
- X **rose from** 20 **to** 45, an increase of 25 units.
- While X increased, Y **remained broadly unchanged**.
- At 60%, A was **three times the proportion of** B.
- After peaking at 45, the figure **edged down** to 42.

Use past tense for completed periods, present tense for a chart with no time reference, and future language only for projections. Do not write “increased by 45” when the value rose *to* 45; that confuses change with final level.

## Common mistakes and repairs
**Listing:** “A was 20. B was 30. C was 40.” Repair it with a comparison: “A and B were lower than C, at 20 and 30 versus 40.”

**Missing overview:** A report can contain accurate details yet lose Task Achievement marks. Write the overview immediately after the introduction.

**Inventing explanations:** “This happened because people preferred…” is speculation. Report the visual, not an imagined cause.

**Mechanical grouping:** Chronological order is not always logical. Group values when that makes a trend clearer.

**Inaccurate approximation:** Use *about, roughly,* or *just over* only when the visual does not support precision. Never alter a clearly labelled number.

## Practice tasks
1. Write a 20-minute report on a graphic in which one category rises from 12% to 48%, two categories remain near 25%, and another falls from 35% to 18%.
2. Create an overview using no numbers for a chart with six categories. Then select five figures that prove it.
3. Rewrite a 170-word report that has no comparisons. Add contrast language without changing the facts.
4. Exchange a report with a partner and check every number against the source.

## Self-assessment checklist
Before submitting, ask: Have I described the visual rather than explained it? Is there a separate overview? Does each body paragraph have a grouping principle? Are all units and comparisons accurate? Have I used a range of precise language naturally? Are there at least 150 words, with no irrelevant conclusion?

### Band 6 sample answer
The graphic shows that four countries are shown for income, electricity use, and life expectancy, with one country leading on all three measures. Overall, there was a clear difference between the main categories. The first measure was generally higher, although the pattern changed near the end. In the first period, the leading figure rose from 20 to 45, while the other value stayed close to 30. It then fell slightly. By the final period, the gap had become smaller. This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.

**Why it earns this level:** This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.
### Band 7 sample answer
The graphic shows that four countries are shown for income, electricity use, and life expectancy, with one country leading on all three measures. Overall, the dominant category increased and finished first, whereas the smaller category was comparatively stable. At the outset, the two measures were 20 and 30 respectively. The leading series then climbed to 45 before easing marginally, while its counterpart remained around 30. Consequently, the difference was widest in the middle of the period. The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.

**Why it earns this level:** The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.
### Band 8 sample answer
The graphic shows that four countries are shown for income, electricity use, and life expectancy, with one country leading on all three measures. Overall, one measure rose markedly to become the clear leader, while the other changed little; the most notable feature was the temporary widening of the gap. Beginning at 20, the first figure more than doubled to 45 before levelling off just below that point. By contrast, the second hovered at approximately 30 throughout. Thus, the series diverged sharply mid-period and remained separated at the close. The response groups information and uses data accurately.

**Why it earns this level:** The response groups information and uses data accurately.
### Band 9 sample answer
The graphic shows that four countries are shown for income, electricity use, and life expectancy, with one country leading on all three measures. Overall, the principal measure expanded substantially, whereas the comparator was virtually static, producing a pronounced and enduring disparity after the midpoint. From a relatively modest base of 20, the former accelerated to 45, then consolidated at a marginally lower level. The latter, however, fluctuated only within a narrow band around 30. The salient pattern is therefore not simply growth, but the transformation from a small initial difference into a sustained lead. Every figure supports the overview rather than appearing as an isolated list.

**Why it earns this level:** Every figure supports the overview rather than appearing as an isolated list.

## Examiner perspective
At Band 6, a candidate usually addresses the task but may select details unevenly or make unclear comparisons. Band 7 reports the main features and organises them logically. Band 8 extends and supports key features with well-chosen detail. Band 9 is fully accurate, sharply selective, cohesive, and effortless to read. The decisive change is not ornate vocabulary; it is better decisions about what matters.

# Chapter 100: Processes

**Part:** 6 — IELTS Writing Task 1 (Academic)


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Purpose and success criteria
Process diagrams explain stages in a manufactured or natural system. Sequence, accuracy, and passive structures are central. These tasks test your ability to select, organise, and compare visual information in at least 150 words. They do not reward specialist knowledge or imaginative explanation. A strong report gives a faithful overview, groups related features, and supports each comparison with accurate data. Aim to plan for three minutes, write for fourteen, and reserve three minutes to check units, tense, articles, and spelling.

## Reliable four-paragraph structure
1. **Introduction:** paraphrase the task in one sentence: chart type, subject, place, and period.
2. **Overview:** state two or three highest-level features. Do not load this paragraph with every number.
3. **Body paragraph 1:** present a logical group, usually the largest values, a shared trend, or the first time period.
4. **Body paragraph 2:** complete the remaining meaningful comparison.

The structure is not a formula for copying. Its purpose is to make the reader see your organisation. If a graphic has two strongly contrasting groups, compare them by group; if it has a clear chronology, compare it by stage.

## How to analyse before writing
Read the title, axes, legend, units, dates, and footnotes. Ask: What is measured? Which feature is highest or lowest? What changes most? Where do categories converge, diverge, overtake, or remain stable? Circle no more than six useful figures. An overview is a judgement about patterns, not a shortened data dump.

For a typical prompt, imagine that coffee beans are harvested, dried, roasted, ground, packaged, and delivered to retailers. Your notes might be: “first measure rises strongly; second remains near 30; widest gap in middle; first still leads at end.” These notes can become an overview. Exact figures belong in the body paragraphs.

## Vocabulary with control
Use words only when their meanings match the evidence.

**Sequence:** initially, subsequently, following this, at the next stage, thereafter, finally. **Process verbs:** undergo, be fed into, be transferred, be filtered, be heated, be stored. **Cycles:** the process then repeats, completing the cycle.

For movement, use a verb plus an optional adverb: *rose gradually, fell sharply, remained broadly stable*. For a static comparison, prefer *stood at, accounted for, was twice as high as, exceeded, lagged behind*. Avoid “dramatically” for a change of one unit and avoid “respectively” unless the order is unmistakable.

## Sentence patterns
- X **stood at** 24%, compared with 18% for Y.
- X **rose from** 20 **to** 45, an increase of 25 units.
- While X increased, Y **remained broadly unchanged**.
- At 60%, A was **three times the proportion of** B.
- After peaking at 45, the figure **edged down** to 42.

Use past tense for completed periods, present tense for a chart with no time reference, and future language only for projections. Do not write “increased by 45” when the value rose *to* 45; that confuses change with final level.

## Common mistakes and repairs
**Listing:** “A was 20. B was 30. C was 40.” Repair it with a comparison: “A and B were lower than C, at 20 and 30 versus 40.”

**Missing overview:** A report can contain accurate details yet lose Task Achievement marks. Write the overview immediately after the introduction.

**Inventing explanations:** “This happened because people preferred…” is speculation. Report the visual, not an imagined cause.

**Mechanical grouping:** Chronological order is not always logical. Group values when that makes a trend clearer.

**Inaccurate approximation:** Use *about, roughly,* or *just over* only when the visual does not support precision. Never alter a clearly labelled number.

## Practice tasks
1. Write a 20-minute report on a graphic in which one category rises from 12% to 48%, two categories remain near 25%, and another falls from 35% to 18%.
2. Create an overview using no numbers for a chart with six categories. Then select five figures that prove it.
3. Rewrite a 170-word report that has no comparisons. Add contrast language without changing the facts.
4. Exchange a report with a partner and check every number against the source.

## Self-assessment checklist
Before submitting, ask: Have I described the visual rather than explained it? Is there a separate overview? Does each body paragraph have a grouping principle? Are all units and comparisons accurate? Have I used a range of precise language naturally? Are there at least 150 words, with no irrelevant conclusion?

### Band 6 sample answer
The graphic shows that coffee beans are harvested, dried, roasted, ground, packaged, and delivered to retailers. Overall, there was a clear difference between the main categories. The first measure was generally higher, although the pattern changed near the end. In the first period, the leading figure rose from 20 to 45, while the other value stayed close to 30. It then fell slightly. By the final period, the gap had become smaller. This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.

**Why it earns this level:** This answer is clear but reports several details separately and uses limited comparison.
### Band 7 sample answer
The graphic shows that coffee beans are harvested, dried, roasted, ground, packaged, and delivered to retailers. Overall, the dominant category increased and finished first, whereas the smaller category was comparatively stable. At the outset, the two measures were 20 and 30 respectively. The leading series then climbed to 45 before easing marginally, while its counterpart remained around 30. Consequently, the difference was widest in the middle of the period. The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.

**Why it earns this level:** The selection is relevant and comparisons are mostly well controlled.
### Band 8 sample answer
The graphic shows that coffee beans are harvested, dried, roasted, ground, packaged, and delivered to retailers. Overall, one measure rose markedly to become the clear leader, while the other changed little; the most notable feature was the temporary widening of the gap. Beginning at 20, the first figure more than doubled to 45 before levelling off just below that point. By contrast, the second hovered at approximately 30 throughout. Thus, the series diverged sharply mid-period and remained separated at the close. The response groups information and uses data accurately.

**Why it earns this level:** The response groups information and uses data accurately.
### Band 9 sample answer
The graphic shows that coffee beans are harvested, dried, roasted, ground, packaged, and delivered to retailers. Overall, the principal measure expanded substantially, whereas the comparator was virtually static, producing a pronounced and enduring disparity after the midpoint. From a relatively modest base of 20, the former accelerated to 45, then consolidated at a marginally lower level. The latter, however, fluctuated only within a narrow band around 30. The salient pattern is therefore not simply growth, but the transformation from a small initial difference into a sustained lead. Every figure supports the overview rather than appearing as an isolated list.

**Why it earns this level:** Every figure supports the overview rather than appearing as an isolated list.

## Examiner perspective
At Band 6, a candidate usually addresses the task but may select details unevenly or make unclear comparisons. Band 7 reports the main features and organises them logically. Band 8 extends and supports key features with well-chosen detail. Band 9 is fully accurate, sharply selective, cohesive, and effortless to read. The decisive change is not ornate vocabulary; it is better decisions about what matters.

Draft two sentences, read them aloud once, and revise only errors you can name. This is deliberate practice: accuracy comes before speed. # Chapter 102: General Training Letters

**Part:** 6 — IELTS Writing Task 1 (General Training)


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## The task
General Training Task 1 asks you to write a letter of at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. The prompt gives a situation and three bullet points. Address every bullet point fully, use a tone that matches the reader, and make the purpose clear from the first paragraph.

## Tone and format
Formal: *Dear Sir or Madam, ... Yours faithfully*. Semi-formal: *Dear Mr Khan, ... Yours sincerely*. Informal: *Dear Sam, ... Best wishes*. A formal complaint needs polite precision, not anger. A message to a friend can use contractions and warmth, but it still needs clear paragraphs.

## Four-part plan
Open with purpose and relevant context. Deal with the first and second bullet points in separate, developed paragraphs. Complete the final point and state an appropriate request, offer, or next action. Plan details before writing: who, what happened, when, impact, and desired outcome.

## Useful language
Formal requests: *I am writing to enquire about; I would be grateful if you could; I would appreciate a response by*. Complaints: *I wish to express my dissatisfaction; the item failed to match the description; I request a replacement or refund*. Informal language: *I thought I’d let you know; would you be able to; it would be great if*.

## Model: formal complaint
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about a bicycle I rented from your Riverside branch on 4 June. Although I booked it for a full day, its rear brake failed within twenty minutes of collection.

When I returned to the branch, the attendant acknowledged that the brake cable was worn but could not provide a replacement. Consequently, I had to cancel a planned trip with visiting relatives and pay for taxis instead. I was particularly disappointed because your website describes every bicycle as safety-checked.

I would therefore like a full refund of the rental fee and reimbursement for the taxi costs, for which I have enclosed receipts. Please confirm how you intend to resolve this matter within seven days.

Yours faithfully,
Alex Morgan

**Examiner comment:** The purpose, all bullet points, suitable formal register, and a clear requested action are developed. Notice that the tone is firm without being rude.

## Practice tasks
1. Write to a college director requesting a timetable change; explain the clash, propose an alternative, and ask about the decision process.
2. Write to a neighbour about a noisy renovation; describe the impact, suggest reasonable hours, and invite a reply.
3. Write to a friend who is moving city; give advice about housing, offer practical help, and arrange a meeting.
4. Write to a hotel after a disappointing stay; explain two problems, say what staff did, and request compensation.

# Chapter 103: Task 1 Practice and Review

**Part:** 6 — IELTS Writing


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## How to use this chapter
Practice improves when it is diagnostic. Do not write ten reports and only count words. Before each task, predict the overview. After writing, mark every comparison, check every unit, and identify one recurring language error. Rewrite one paragraph rather than merely reading feedback.

## Academic practice set
1. A line graph shows the number of electric and petrol cars sold in three countries between 2012 and 2024.
2. A bar chart compares weekly hours spent on paid work, childcare, and leisure by men and women in 1995 and 2025.
3. Two pie charts show sources of electricity in a region in 2005 and 2025.
4. A table gives population, urban share, and average income in five cities.
5. Two maps show a library site before and after renovation.
6. A process diagram illustrates how discarded glass is recycled into new containers.
7. A combined bar and line chart shows advertising spend and online sales over six years.

## General Training practice set
1. Write to your manager to request training leave. Explain the course, how it benefits work, and how duties will be covered.
2. Write to a local council about a dangerous crossing. Describe the problem, explain who is affected, and suggest a solution.
3. Write to a friend who has offered accommodation. Thank them, explain your arrival plans, and ask one practical question.

## Review rubric
Task response: Is every required feature or bullet point developed? Organisation: Does each paragraph have a purpose? Vocabulary: Are words precise and natural? Grammar: Are complex sentences controlled? Make an error log with columns for error, correction, reason, and personal example.

## Timed cycle
Use three minutes to analyse, fourteen to write, and three to edit. On a second attempt, reduce planning to two minutes only after you can consistently identify the overview. Never cut editing time; a correction to subject–verb agreement or a data unit can protect several marks.

# Chapter 104: Writing Task 2 Overview

**Part:** 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## The task and marking
Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes. Task Response assesses whether you answer every part and develop ideas; Coherence and Cohesion assesses organisation; Lexical Resource assesses precise, flexible vocabulary; Grammatical Range and Accuracy assesses controlled sentence variety. Task 2 carries more weight than Task 1, so manage time accordingly.

## A dependable workflow
Spend five minutes interpreting the question and planning. Write an introduction, two developed body paragraphs, and a conclusion in roughly thirty minutes. Reserve five minutes to check that your position is consistent, both parts are answered, and grammar is accurate. Two strong ideas are safer than four thin ones.

## The thesis test
Your thesis must answer the exact wording. For “discuss both views and give your opinion,” name both views and give your own judgement. For “what problems and what solutions,” give both. For a two-part question, do not let one paragraph become a general discussion while another question disappears.

## Development over decoration
Each body paragraph needs a claim, why it is true, an example, and why the example matters. Avoid memorised hooks, quotations, and imaginary statistics. Logical development produces cohesion: use a connector only when it names a real relationship.

## Editing priorities
Check subject–verb agreement, articles, singular/plural nouns, verb forms, pronoun reference, and punctuation around dependent clauses. Then replace one vague word with an exact one. Do not rewrite whole paragraphs in the final minutes.

# Chapter 105: Opinion Essays

**Part:** 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## What the question requires
Choose a clear position, acknowledge a reasonable limitation, and defend it consistently. The question is: **Some people believe that governments should make university education free for everyone. To what extent do you agree or disagree?** Read it twice. Underline the task words, identify whether it asks for reasons, effects, solutions, comparison, evaluation, or your opinion, and make a one-sentence answer before planning examples. A sophisticated essay that answers a different question cannot score highly for Task Response.

## Flexible template
**Introduction:** paraphrase the issue and give a direct thesis.  
**Body paragraph 1:** topic sentence, explanation, specific example, and consequence.  
**Body paragraph 2:** a distinct main point developed in the same way; include a concession if it improves accuracy.  
**Conclusion:** restate the judgement or answer in fresh language.  

This is a planning scaffold, not text to memorise. Examiners recognise empty openings such as “This essay will discuss both sides.” Your thesis should contain meaning: “Although free tuition widens access, a targeted scheme is more sustainable than universal funding.”

## Planning in five minutes
Write P (position), A and B (two reasons), E (one realistic example for each), and C (a concession). Then test your ideas: can each be explained beyond one sentence? Is it directly relevant? Does the example illustrate rather than replace reasoning? Prefer a narrow, plausible example over an invented statistic.

## Paragraph architecture
A useful paragraph moves from claim to mechanism to illustration to implication. For example: “Targeted grants improve access because they remove the financial barrier for students from low-income households. A trainee nurse who can cover tuition and transport is less likely to abandon a course for paid work. This approach therefore broadens participation without subsidising affluent families who can already pay.” The example is specific, but no unverified number is needed.

## Linking without mechanical signals
Use logical relationships, not a chain of *firstly, secondly, finally*. Addition: *moreover, equally important*. Contrast: *however, nevertheless, whereas*. Cause: *therefore, consequently, which means that*. Concession: *admittedly, although, even if*. Reference words such as *this approach, such pressure,* and *the latter* can create cohesion when their referent is clear.

## Lexis and grammar
Favour precise collocations: *allocate public funds, widen access, impose a burden, mitigate a risk, foster independence*. Use complex grammar to express real relationships: “If employers subsidised retraining, displaced workers could move into growing sectors.” Accuracy matters more than density. Avoid absolute claims such as “technology always improves education.”

## Band 9 model
Some people believe that governments should make university education free for everyone. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

People often frame this issue as a choice between two simple alternatives. In reality, the strongest policy combines a clear principle with practical limits. I take the view that public action is justified when it removes a genuine barrier to opportunity, but it should be designed to concentrate help where it produces the greatest social return.

The principal reason is that unequal access can reproduce disadvantage across generations. When a capable student cannot pursue training because basic fees and living costs are unaffordable, society loses both that individual’s potential and the services they might later provide. Targeted support, for instance, can enable students from low-income households to enter shortage professions without transferring an unnecessary subsidy to families who could fund the same education privately.

Admittedly, universal provision is administratively simple and avoids the stigma sometimes attached to means testing. Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

## Examiner comment
The model gives a direct, nuanced position, develops two connected reasons, and uses an example to clarify a mechanism. Cohesion comes from ideas and reference, not excessive connectors. Vocabulary is precise but not ornamental, and complex sentences remain controlled. A Band 9 response still needs to be accurate, relevant, and natural; length or difficult words alone do not create the score.

## Common mistakes
**Partial answer:** answering only one part of a two-part question. Label each part in your plan.  
**Undeveloped lists:** naming three ideas but explaining none. Use two fully developed points.  
**Memorised language:** forcing an irrelevant phrase or quotation. Write what the question needs.  
**False evidence:** inventing research or statistics. Use plausible examples without pretending authority.  
**New ideas in the conclusion:** conclude; do not begin a third body paragraph.

## Practice questions
1. Governments should spend more on preventing illness than treating it. Discuss.
2. Children should begin formal education earlier. To what extent do you agree?
3. International tourism has more disadvantages than advantages. Discuss both views.
4. Why do many people change careers several times, and is this positive?
5. Should employers be required to offer flexible working arrangements?

**Part:** 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2


<div class="chapter-meta">

## What the question requires
Represent both views fairly before making your own position unmistakable. The question is: **Some people think remote work benefits society, while others believe it damages communities. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.** Read it twice. Underline the task words, identify whether it asks for reasons, effects, solutions, comparison, evaluation, or your opinion, and make a one-sentence answer before planning examples. A sophisticated essay that answers a different question cannot score highly for Task Response.

## Flexible template
**Introduction:** paraphrase the issue and give a direct thesis.  
**Body paragraph 1:** topic sentence, explanation, specific example, and consequence.  
**Body paragraph 2:** a distinct main point developed in the same way; include a concession if it improves accuracy.  
**Conclusion:** restate the judgement or answer in fresh language.  

This is a planning scaffold, not text to memorise. Examiners recognise empty openings such as “This essay will discuss both sides.” Your thesis should contain meaning: “Although free tuition widens access, a targeted scheme is more sustainable than universal funding.”

## Planning in five minutes
Write P (position), A and B (two reasons), E (one realistic example for each), and C (a concession). Then test your ideas: can each be explained beyond one sentence? Is it directly relevant? Does the example illustrate rather than replace reasoning? Prefer a narrow, plausible example over an invented statistic.

## Paragraph architecture
A useful paragraph moves from claim to mechanism to illustration to implication. For example: “Targeted grants improve access because they remove the financial barrier for students from low-income households. A trainee nurse who can cover tuition and transport is less likely to abandon a course for paid work. This approach therefore broadens participation without subsidising affluent families who can already pay.” The example is specific, but no unverified number is needed.

## Linking without mechanical signals
Use logical relationships, not a chain of *firstly, secondly, finally*. Addition: *moreover, equally important*. Contrast: *however, nevertheless, whereas*. Cause: *therefore, consequently, which means that*. Concession: *admittedly, although, even if*. Reference words such as *this approach, such pressure,* and *the latter* can create cohesion when their referent is clear.

## Lexis and grammar
Favour precise collocations: *allocate public funds, widen access, impose a burden, mitigate a risk, foster independence*. Use complex grammar to express real relationships: “If employers subsidised retraining, displaced workers could move into growing sectors.” Accuracy matters more than density. Avoid absolute claims such as “technology always improves education.”

## Band 9 model
Some people think remote work benefits society, while others believe it damages communities. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

People often frame this issue as a choice between two simple alternatives. In reality, the strongest policy combines a clear principle with practical limits. I take the view that public action is justified when it removes a genuine barrier to opportunity, but it should be designed to concentrate help where it produces the greatest social return.

The principal reason is that unequal access can reproduce disadvantage across generations. When a capable student cannot pursue training because basic fees and living costs are unaffordable, society loses both that individual’s potential and the services they might later provide. Targeted support, for instance, can enable students from low-income households to enter shortage professions without transferring an unnecessary subsidy to families who could fund the same education privately.

Admittedly, universal provision is administratively simple and avoids the stigma sometimes attached to means testing. Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

## Examiner comment
The model gives a direct, nuanced position, develops two connected reasons, and uses an example to clarify a mechanism. Cohesion comes from ideas and reference, not excessive connectors. Vocabulary is precise but not ornamental, and complex sentences remain controlled. A Band 9 response still needs to be accurate, relevant, and natural; length or difficult words alone do not create the score.

## Common mistakes
**Partial answer:** answering only one part of a two-part question. Label each part in your plan.  
**Undeveloped lists:** naming three ideas but explaining none. Use two fully developed points.  
**Memorised language:** forcing an irrelevant phrase or quotation. Write what the question needs.  
**False evidence:** inventing research or statistics. Use plausible examples without pretending authority.  
**New ideas in the conclusion:** conclude; do not begin a third body paragraph.

## Practice questions
1. Governments should spend more on preventing illness than treating it. Discuss.
2. Children should begin formal education earlier. To what extent do you agree?
3. International tourism has more disadvantages than advantages. Discuss both views.
4. Why do many people change careers several times, and is this positive?
5. Should employers be required to offer flexible working arrangements?

Cause: *therefore, consequently, which means that*. Concession: *admittedly, although, even if*. Reference words such as *this approach, such pressure,* and *the latter* can create cohesion when their referent is clear.

## Lexis and grammar
Favour precise collocations: *allocate public funds, widen access, impose a burden, mitigate a risk, foster independence*. Use complex grammar to express real relationships: “If employers subsidised retraining, displaced workers could move into growing sectors.” Accuracy matters more than density. Avoid absolute claims such as “technology always improves education.”

## Band 9 model
More schools are replacing printed textbooks with digital devices. Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?

People often frame this issue as a choice between two simple alternatives. In reality, the strongest policy combines a clear principle with practical limits. I take the view that public action is justified when it removes a genuine barrier to opportunity, but it should be designed to concentrate help where it produces the greatest social return.

The principal reason is that unequal access can reproduce disadvantage across generations. When a capable student cannot pursue training because basic fees and living costs are unaffordable, society loses both that individual’s potential and the services they might later provide. Targeted support, for instance, can enable students from low-income households to enter shortage professions without transferring an unnecessary subsidy to families who could fund the same education privately.

Admittedly, universal provision is administratively simple and avoids the stigma sometimes attached to means testing. Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

## Examiner comment
The model gives a direct, nuanced position, develops two connected reasons, and uses an example to clarify a mechanism. Cohesion comes from ideas and reference, not excessive connectors. Vocabulary is precise but not ornamental, and complex sentences remain controlled. A Band 9 response still needs to be accurate, relevant, and natural; length or difficult words alone do not create the score.

## Common mistakes
**Partial answer:** answering only one part of a two-part question. Label each part in your plan.  
**Undeveloped lists:** naming three ideas but explaining none. Use two fully developed points.  
**Memorised language:** forcing an irrelevant phrase or quotation. Write what the question needs.  
**False evidence:** inventing research or statistics. Use plausible examples without pretending authority.  
**New ideas in the conclusion:** conclude; do not begin a third body paragraph.

2. Children should begin formal education earlier. To what extent do you agree?
3. International tourism has more disadvantages than advantages. Discuss both views.
4. Why do many people change careers several times, and is this positive?
5. Should employers be required to offer flexible working arrangements?

# Chapter 109: Double-Question Essays

**Part:** 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## What the question requires
Answer each question directly while making the relation between the paragraphs explicit. The question is: **In many countries, young adults delay buying a home. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?** Read it twice. Underline the task words, identify whether it asks for reasons, effects, solutions, comparison, evaluation, or your opinion, and make a one-sentence answer before planning examples. A sophisticated essay that answers a different question cannot score highly for Task Response.

## Flexible template
**Introduction:** paraphrase the issue and give a direct thesis.  
**Body paragraph 1:** topic sentence, explanation, specific example, and consequence.  
**Body paragraph 2:** a distinct main point developed in the same way; include a concession if it improves accuracy.  
**Conclusion:** restate the judgement or answer in fresh language.  

This is a planning scaffold, not text to memorise. Examiners recognise empty openings such as “This essay will discuss both sides.” Your thesis should contain meaning: “Although free tuition widens access, a targeted scheme is more sustainable than universal funding.”

## Planning in five minutes
Write P (position), A and B (two reasons), E (one realistic example for each), and C (a concession). Then test your ideas: can each be explained beyond one sentence? Is it directly relevant? Does the example illustrate rather than replace reasoning? Prefer a narrow, plausible example over an invented statistic.

## Paragraph architecture
A useful paragraph moves from claim to mechanism to illustration to implication. For example: “Targeted grants improve access because they remove the financial barrier for students from low-income households. A trainee nurse who can cover tuition and transport is less likely to abandon a course for paid work. This approach therefore broadens participation without subsidising affluent families who can already pay.” The example is specific, but no unverified number is needed.

## Linking without mechanical signals
Use logical relationships, not a chain of *firstly, secondly, finally*. Addition: *moreover, equally important*. Contrast: *however, nevertheless, whereas*. Cause: *therefore, consequently, which means that*. Concession: *admittedly, although, even if*. Reference words such as *this approach, such pressure,* and *the latter* can create cohesion when their referent is clear.

## Lexis and grammar

Use complex grammar to express real relationships: “If employers subsidised retraining, displaced workers could move into growing sectors.” Accuracy matters more than density. Avoid absolute claims such as “technology always improves education.”

Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

# Chapter 110: Cohesion and Lexis

**Part:** 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Cohesion is logical visibility
Cohesion helps the reader follow your reasoning. It is not a competition to use the largest number of linkers. A paragraph is cohesive when its sentences answer a sequence: claim, reason, example, consequence. Repeating a key noun selectively is often clearer than replacing it with an ambiguous synonym.

## Four cohesive tools
**Reference:** “This policy” must point to one identifiable policy.  
**Substitution:** use *this approach, such a measure,* or *the former* when the reference is unmistakable.  
**Conjunction:** choose *however, therefore, for example,* and *although* for their real logical function.  
**Lexical chains:** repeat a controlled family: *housing, rent, tenants, affordability*, rather than jumping among unrelated fancy synonyms.

## Lexical resource
Band 7 vocabulary is generally flexible and accurate. Band 8–9 vocabulary is more precise and natural, with rare slips. Precision means writing *mitigate traffic congestion* rather than *make traffic badness lower*. Collocation matters: *pose a threat, allocate funding, draw a distinction, address a shortfall, impose a restriction*.

## Repair exercise
Weak: “Firstly, people use phones. Moreover, phones are bad. On the other hand, phones are useful.”  
Better: “Constant phone use can fragment attention, particularly when notifications interrupt sustained study. Nevertheless, the same devices allow students to access course materials and contact tutors quickly. Their value therefore depends on whether users can control interruptions.”

## Practice
Rewrite ten old paragraphs by removing half their connectors. Add only those needed to express contrast, result, illustration, or concession. Build themed word banks from your own essays and record a collocation, a sentence, and a common error for each item.

# Chapter 111: Band Comparisons

**Part:** 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## One idea at four levels
Question: Should cities restrict private cars in central areas?

**Band 6:** “Cars cause pollution, so cities should restrict them. People can use buses.” The position is clear but explanation is brief and vocabulary is general.

**Band 7:** “Cities should restrict private cars because concentrated traffic worsens air quality and delays buses. A congestion charge can encourage commuters to use public transport.” The claim is developed and relevant.

**Band 8:** “Restricting private cars in dense centres can improve both air quality and the reliability of buses, which otherwise become trapped in the same congestion. Charging drivers at peak times gives commuters a financial reason to shift journeys.” The mechanism is clear and language is precise.

**Band 9:** “In compact city centres, limiting private vehicles is justified because each additional car consumes scarce road space while slowing buses that carry far more passengers. A peak-time charge, paired with frequent affordable public transport, can therefore reduce emissions without simply transferring inconvenience to lower-income commuters.” The response is nuanced, well developed, and grammatically controlled.

## What changes across bands
Higher bands do not merely add longer sentences. They answer every part, choose ideas that can be explained, connect claims to consequences, use accurate collocations, and make very few errors. Improve one dimension at a time: first relevance, then development, then paragraph cohesion, then language precision.

## Diagnostic routine
Take a recent essay. Highlight thesis statements in blue, explanations in green, examples in yellow, and unsupported assertions in red. If red dominates, develop fewer ideas. Then check whether each pronoun has a clear noun and whether every connector expresses its stated relationship.

Draft two sentences, read them aloud once, and revise only errors you can name. This is deliberate practice: accuracy comes before speed. Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. On the next attempt, use a new data point or idea so that you practise transfer rather than memorisation.

## How to use this bank
Plan rather than memorise. For each question, identify the type, write a one-sentence thesis, select two ideas, and test whether you answer every instruction. Rotate topics and question types. All questions below are original practice prompts.

## Questions
1. Education: To what extent should governments give greater priority to schools?
2. Education: What factors are currently shaping schools, and what effects do these changes have?
3. Education: Discuss two contrasting views about schools and give your own opinion.
4. Education: Do the advantages of recent developments in schools outweigh the disadvantages?
5. Education: Why are patterns relating to schools changing, and is this a positive or negative development?
6. Education: What problems are associated with schools, and what practical solutions can be proposed?

## Deliberate-practice rotation
Choose ten questions per week: two opinion, two discussion, two problem–solution, two advantage–disadvantage, and two double questions. Write full essays for three, outlines for four, and introductions plus theses for three. Revisit weak topics after feedback.

# Chapter 113: Band 9 Model Answers and Examiner Comments

**Part:** 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |

| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |

</div>

## How to learn from a model
Do not memorise these responses. Read the question, predict a position and two reasons, then compare your plan with the model. Underline the thesis, topic sentences, explanations, examples, concessions, and conclusion. A model is useful when it teaches decisions, not when it becomes borrowed language.

## Model 1: public transport
**Question:** Governments should make public transport free in all cities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Free public transport is an attractive proposal because it could reduce the cost of daily travel. However, I do not agree that it should be universally free. A low fare combined with substantial investment in reliability is a more equitable and sustainable policy.

The strongest case for free services is that price can exclude low-income residents from employment, education, and healthcare. When a family must choose between travel and essentials, a fare reduction can have an immediate effect on opportunity. In addition, cheaper buses and trains may persuade some drivers to leave their cars at home, easing congestion and emissions.

Nevertheless, abolishing fares does not itself create a useful network. If services are infrequent, overcrowded, or unavailable outside central areas, many commuters will still need private vehicles. Funding every journey from general taxation may also divert money from maintenance and route expansion. A better approach is to cap fares for regular users and provide free travel for people with demonstrable need, while directing remaining funds towards frequent, accessible services.

In conclusion, affordability matters, but completely free transport is not necessarily the best use of public money. Targeted concessions and high-quality provision would serve both fairness and long-term demand.

**Examiner comment:** The answer maintains a qualified position throughout, develops a counterargument fairly, and evaluates policy by practical criteria. Lexis such as *route expansion* and *targeted concessions* is precise, while grammar is varied and accurate.

## Model 2: remote work
**Question:** More people work from home than in the past. What are the reasons, and is this a positive or negative development?

Working from home has expanded because digital tools now allow many tasks to be completed away from a traditional office, while employers have recognised that physical presence is not always necessary. On balance, this is a positive development, provided workers retain regular contact with colleagues.

The technical reason is straightforward: cloud-based files, video meetings, and secure communication platforms allow teams to coordinate across locations. Employers also save on office space, and staff may avoid long daily commutes. These incentives became visible when organisations were forced to adopt remote systems and later discovered that routine work could continue effectively.

The principal benefit is greater control over time. A parent, for example, may arrange work around school hours without sacrificing employment altogether. Fewer commuting journeys can also reduce pressure on transport networks. Admittedly, isolation and blurred boundaries can harm wellbeing, especially for new employees who need informal guidance. Companies should therefore offer hybrid arrangements, regular mentoring, and a clear right to disconnect.

Overall, remote work is beneficial because it broadens flexibility and can reduce wasted travel. Its advantages depend, however, on deliberate measures to preserve collaboration and protect personal time.

**Examiner comment:** Both parts are answered directly. The response explains mechanisms, offers a realistic example, and makes a balanced evaluation rather than treating the trend as wholly positive.

## Model 3: school assessment
**Question:** Some people think examinations are the best way to assess students, while others believe continuous assessment is better. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

Examinations remain popular because they test students under identical conditions, whereas continuous assessment captures performance over a longer period. Although formal exams have a role, I believe a carefully moderated combination of both methods is the fairest approach.

Supporters of examinations argue that a single standardised test limits the influence of teachers’ personal judgement. Students answer the same questions in the same time, making results easier to compare across schools. This can be particularly important for university admission, where institutions need a transparent basis for selecting applicants.

Continuous assessment, however, measures skills that a timed exam may miss. Research projects, presentations, and drafts show whether learners can apply knowledge, respond to feedback, and complete sustained work. They also reduce the risk that illness or anxiety on one day will determine an entire grade. The weakness is that standards can vary, so external moderation is necessary.

In conclusion, examinations offer comparability, while continuous assessment gives a fuller picture of learning. Schools should use both, with common criteria and moderation to protect consistency.

**Examiner comment:** Each view receives a developed paragraph, and the personal view is clear in both introduction and conclusion. The writer avoids unsupported claims and uses a concession to produce a nuanced judgement.

## Model 4: food waste
**Question:** Food waste is increasing in many countries. What problems does this cause, and what can be done?

Rising food waste damages the environment and places unnecessary pressure on household budgets. The problem can be reduced through clearer information, improved retail practices, and systems that redirect edible surplus.

When food is discarded, the water, energy, and labour used to produce and transport it are wasted as well. Disposal creates further emissions, particularly where organic matter is sent to landfill. At household level, frequent disposal often reflects poor planning: consumers buy perishable goods without considering what they already have or when they will use it.

Governments can require clearer date labels that distinguish safety from quality, since many people discard food that remains edible. Retailers should also discount items approaching their use-by date and partner with charities to redistribute safe surplus. Finally, schools and public campaigns can teach practical skills such as meal planning and storage. Together, these measures reduce waste before it reaches the bin rather than relying solely on recycling afterwards.

In conclusion, food waste has environmental and financial costs, but it is not inevitable. Better information and coordinated action by households, shops, and authorities can address it at several stages.

**Examiner comment:** The essay answers problems and solutions in balanced depth. The solutions are specific, feasible, and explicitly linked to the causes.

### Timed refinement drill 1: identify the central comparison before writing
In a Band 9 model analysis response, spend two minutes on this controlled exercise. Write one overview sentence that names the largest contrast, then test whether every detail paragraph supports it.
Draft two sentences, read them aloud once, and revise only errors you can name. This is deliberate practice: accuracy comes before speed. Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. On the next attempt, use a new data point or idea so that you practise transfer rather than memorisation.

### Timed refinement drill 2: separate a fact from an inference
In a Band 9 model analysis response, spend two minutes on this controlled exercise. Underline the supplied figures. Report only what the visual or question establishes; do not explain a cause unless the task asks for one.
Draft two sentences, read them aloud once, and revise only errors you can name. This is deliberate practice: accuracy comes before speed. Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. On the next attempt, use a new data point or idea so that you practise transfer rather than memorisation.

Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. On the next attempt, use a new data point or idea so that you practise transfer rather than memorisation.
