# Chapter 114: IELTS Speaking Overview & Format

**Part:** Part 8 — Speaking

---


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Describe the full IELTS Speaking test structure, timing, and scoring criteria for Academic and General Training.
- Explain how the four assessment criteria interact and why a high vocabulary score cannot compensate for poor fluency.
- Predict the sequence and purpose of Parts 1, 2, and 3 and prepare appropriate strategies for each.
- Apply a pre-test, during-test, and post-test routine that reduces anxiety and protects performance.
- Diagnose your personal Speaking profile across Fluency, Lexical Resource, Grammar, and Pronunciation.
- Integrate Speaking practice with vocabulary, grammar, and listening work from earlier parts of this book.
- Set realistic band targets based on observable behaviours rather than self-perceived fluency.

---

## Theory / Explanation

### 114.1 What IELTS Speaking Measures

IELTS Speaking is a **face-to-face oral interview** with a certified examiner. It lasts **11–14 minutes** and assesses your ability to communicate in English across familiar and abstract topics. You are not tested on factual knowledge of IELTS topics; you are tested on whether you can:

1. **Express opinions and information** clearly and coherently.
2. **Develop answers** beyond one-word or memorised responses.
3. **Use a range of vocabulary and grammar** appropriate to the context.
4. **Be understood** without excessive listener effort.
5. **Handle follow-up questions** and more abstract discussion in Part 3.

The same Speaking test format is used for **Academic** and **General Training** candidates. Your Speaking score contributes equally to both versions.

### 114.2 Test Structure at a Glance

| Feature | Detail |
|---------|--------|
| Format | One-to-one interview with examiner |
| Duration | 11–14 minutes total |
| Parts | 3 (Introduction → Long turn → Discussion) |
| Recording | Audio recorded for quality monitoring |
| Scoring | Four criteria, each 25% of final band |
| Result | Single overall band (half-band increments) |

**The three-part architecture:**

| Part | Duration | Format | Purpose |
|------|----------|--------|---------|
| Part 1 | 4–5 min | Short questions on familiar topics | Warm-up; basic fluency and coherence |
| Part 2 | 3–4 min | 1-min prep + 1–2 min monologue on cue card | Sustained speech; organisation |
| Part 3 | 4–5 min | Two-way discussion linked to Part 2 theme | Abstract ideas; justification and speculation |

**Why the structure matters:** Part 1 feels conversational but is still assessed. Part 2 is the only time you speak uninterrupted at length — organisation here strongly signals Band 7+. Part 3 separates candidates who can only describe personal experience from those who can analyse and evaluate ideas.

### 114.3 The Four Assessment Criteria

Your final band is **not** an average of four separate scores visible to you; the examiner produces **one holistic band** informed by four equal-weight criteria:

#### Fluency and Coherence (FC)

- Speaks at length without unnatural pauses
- Uses connectives and discourse markers appropriately
- Develops topics logically; easy to follow

#### Lexical Resource (LR)

- Uses vocabulary flexibly and precisely
- Paraphrases effectively when needed
- Uses less common items with awareness of collocation and style

#### Grammatical Range and Accuracy (GRA)

- Produces a mix of simple and complex structures
- Maintains control; errors are rare and do not impede communication

#### Pronunciation (P)

- Individual sounds, word stress, sentence stress, and intonation are clear
- Can be understood throughout; accent is not penalised if intelligible

**Critical insight:** Weakness in one criterion **caps** your overall performance. A candidate with Band 9 vocabulary but Band 5 fluency (long freezes, reformulating every sentence) will not receive Band 8 overall. Examiners balance criteria; they do not reward isolated strengths.

### 114.4 How Bands Are Assigned

Examiners use **public band descriptors** (see Part 1, Chapter 3). They do not compare you to other candidates on your test day; they compare your performance to descriptor statements.

**Observable differences:**

| Band | Typical performance |
|------|---------------------|
| 5 | Short answers; frequent repetition; limited vocabulary; errors cause some strain |
| 6 | Willing to speak at length but coherence may break; adequate vocabulary; mixed grammar control |
| 7 | Speaks at length with occasional hesitation; uses less common vocabulary; complex structures with some errors |
| 8 | Fluent with only occasional repetition; wide vocabulary; majority of sentences error-free |
| 9 | Fully fluent; precise vocabulary; flexible grammar; effortless intelligibility |

**Half bands:** Examiners may award 6.5, 7.5, etc., when performance sits between descriptor levels.

### 114.5 Part 1: Introduction and Interview

The examiner verifies your identity, then asks **4–12 questions** across **2–3 familiar topic areas** (home, work/study, hobbies, daily routines, transport, etc.).

**Characteristics:**
- Questions are closed and open: *"Do you work or study?"* → *"What do you enjoy about your job?"*
- Answers typically need **2–4 sentences**, not essays.
- Follow-up questions probe the same topic before switching.

**Strategic implication:** Part 1 sets the tone. One-word answers signal low band; over-long monologues waste time and feel unnatural.

### 114.6 Part 2: Individual Long Turn

You receive a **cue card** with a topic and bullet points. You have **1 minute to prepare** (paper and pencil provided) and must speak for **1–2 minutes**. The examiner stops you at 2 minutes.

**Typical cue card structure:**
- Main prompt: *"Describe a place you visited that impressed you."*
- Bullet points: where / when / who with / why it impressed you
- Optional final line: *"And explain whether you would recommend it."*

After your long turn, the examiner asks **1–2 brief follow-up questions** (rounding-off questions).

**Strategic implication:** Notes during preparation are essential. A clear structure (past → detail → opinion) prevents mid-speech panic.

### 114.7 Part 3: Two-Way Discussion

Part 3 questions **extend the Part 2 theme** to society, trends, comparisons, and hypotheticals. Questions become more abstract: *"Why do people enjoy travelling to historical sites?"* → *"Should governments charge higher fees for tourist attractions?"*

**Characteristics:**
- Answers require **4–6 sentences** with explanation and examples.
- Examiners may challenge or redirect: *"Why do you think that?"*
- Speculation and balanced views are valued at higher bands.

**Strategic implication:** Part 3 rewards the same skills as Writing Task 2 — developing ideas, qualifying claims, using examples — but **orally and under time pressure**.

### 114.8 What Examiners Are Not Assessing

Understanding what **does not** affect your score prevents wasted effort:

| Not assessed | Why it matters |
|--------------|----------------|
| Your accent origin | Intelligibility matters; native-like accent does not |
| Whether the examiner agrees with you | No "correct" opinion on abstract topics |
| Body language (mostly) | Assessed on speech; minimal eye contact alone won't fail you |
| Factual accuracy of personal stories | Invent plausible examples if needed |
| British vs American vocabulary | Both acceptable if natural and accurate |

**What *is* penalised:** Memorised scripts detected by unnatural delivery; answers that ignore the question; silence beyond brief thinking pauses.

### 114.9 Test-Day Procedure

1. **Check-in:** ID verification; belongings stored per centre rules.
2. **Waiting:** You may speak to other candidates; stay calm.
3. **Entry:** Examiner greets you; recording begins.
4. **ID check:** Name, candidate number, nationality confirmation.
5. **Parts 1–3:** Continuous interview; no breaks between parts.
6. **End:** Examiner thanks you; you leave. No instant score.

**Recording:** All tests are recorded. A senior examiner may re-mark a sample for quality assurance. This protects **you** as well as standardises marking.

### 114.10 Computer-Delivered vs Paper-Based Speaking

Speaking is **always face-to-face** with a human examiner — even when Listening, Reading, and Writing are computer-delivered. Some centres offer **video-call Speaking** (IELTS Online) with the same format and criteria.

**Implication:** Practice with real humans, not only AI apps. Apps help with drills; they cannot replicate examiner follow-ups or Part 3 pressure.

### 114.11 Common Failure Patterns

| Pattern | Symptom | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| Part 1 minimalism | "Yes." / "No." / "Sometimes." | Extend with reason + example rule |
| Part 2 under-length | Stops at 45 seconds | Structured notes; practise timing |
| Part 2 over-memorisation | Robotic delivery; wrong topic fit | Flexible templates, not scripts |
| Part 3 essay mode | 90-second answers; examiner interrupts | Answer directly, then develop |
| Vocabulary panic | Long pauses searching for "Band 9 words" | Paraphrase simply; upgrade after |
| Grammar freeze | Only short simple sentences | Pre-practise complex patterns safely |
| Pronunciation rush | Mumbling to hide errors | Slow down; stress key words |

### 114.12 Integration with Other Modules

Speaking connects directly to:

- **Listening (Part 4):** Accent exposure, signpost language, natural rhythm.
- **Vocabulary (Part 3):** Topic lexis (Chapters 45–70) feeds Part 3 depth.
- **Grammar (Part 2):** Tense control, conditionals, relative clauses for complex answers.
- **Writing Task 2 (Part 7):** Idea development, paragraph logic transfers to Part 3.

**Weekly integration drill:** After each Speaking mock, extract 10 useful phrases into your vocabulary notebook and recycle them in Writing.

### 114.13 Building a Speaking Study Cycle

**Phase A — Component drills (daily 15–20 min):**
- Pronunciation focus (Chapter 121)
- Fluency extension (Chapter 122)
- Part 1/2/3 strategy chapters (115, 117, 119)

**Phase B — Timed simulation (2–3× weekly):**
- Full mock with partner or tutor
- Record and self-assess against four criteria

**Phase C — Exam simulation:**
- Unfamiliar examiner/partner
- Strict timing including 1-minute Part 2 prep
- Post-mortem error log by criterion

---

## Examples

### Example 1: Part 1 Question Ladder

**Examiner:** "Do you live in a house or an apartment?"  
**Weak:** "Apartment."  
**Strong:** "I live in a rented apartment in the city centre — it's a two-bedroom flat on the fourth floor, which suits me because I'm close to work."

**Examiner (follow-up):** "What's your favourite room?"  
**Strong:** "Probably the balcony, actually. It's small, but I keep plants there, and it's where I drink coffee before starting work."

### Example 2: Part 2 Cue Card (Extract)

> **Describe a skill you learned that you found useful.**  
> You should say:  
> - what the skill was  
> - when and how you learned it  
> - who helped you  
> and explain why it has been useful for you.

**Note structure (1 minute):**
- Skill: basic coding (Python)
- When: university, second year, online course
- How: weekly projects; friend mentor
- Useful: automates spreadsheet tasks at work

### Example 3: Part 3 Escalation

**Part 2 theme:** A useful skill.

**Part 3 questions (increasing abstraction):**
1. "What skills do you think children should learn at school?" (general)
2. "Are practical skills more important than academic subjects?" (comparison)
3. "How might technology change the skills people need in the future?" (speculation)

---

## Worked Examples

### Worked Example 1: Diagnosing a Band 6.0 Plateau

**Profile:** Candidate feels "fluent" in daily life; mock score 6.0; target 7.0.

**Mock observations:**
- Part 1: Good length but repetitive *"I think… I think…"*
- Part 2: 1 minute 10 seconds; lost thread after example
- Part 3: Ideas present but no examples; grammar errors on third conditional

**Diagnosis:** Fluency/Coherence and GRA limit the score; LR is adequate.

**Plan:** Chapter 122 fluency drills; Part 2 timing practice 3× weekly; conditional review (Chapter 26); record and count discourse marker variety.

### Worked Example 2: Criteria Trade-Off

**Scenario:** Candidate uses advanced vocabulary (*" ramifications," " ubiquitous"*) but mispronounces them and pauses 3 seconds before each.

**Examiner perspective:** LR attempt is noted, but FC and P suffer; overall band likely **6.0–6.5**, not 7.5.

**Fix:** Master pronunciation of words you use (Chapter 121); prefer simpler accurate lexis under pressure.

### Worked Example 3: Part 2 Timing Map

**Target:** 2 minutes ≈ 240–280 words at natural pace.

| Segment | Time | Content |
|---------|------|---------|
| Opening | 0:00–0:20 | State topic + context |
| Body point 1 | 0:20–0:50 | First bullet with detail |
| Body point 2 | 0:50–1:20 | Second bullet + sensory detail |
| Body point 3 | 1:20–1:45 | Third bullet / who helped |
| Closing | 1:45–2:00 | Why useful + recommendation |

---

## Practice Exercises

### Exercise Set A — Format Knowledge (Questions 1–15)

1. How many parts are in IELTS Speaking?
2. How long is Part 2 preparation time?
3. Minimum time you should aim to speak in Part 2?
4. Name the four assessment criteria.
5. Is Speaking different for Academic vs General Training?
6. What happens at the start of the test regarding recording?
7. Which part involves a cue card?
8. Are you penalised for an accent?
9. What is a "rounding-off question"?
10. How long is the full Speaking test?
11. Which criterion covers discourse markers?
12. Can you ask the examiner to explain a Part 3 question?
13. What materials are given in Part 2 prep?
14. Does the examiner score each part separately?
15. Is there a penalty for saying "I don't know"?

### Exercise Set B — Criteria Mapping (Questions 16–22)

For each error, identify the **primary** criterion affected (FC, LR, GRA, P):

16. Speaker repeats "very very very" while thinking.
17. Says *"childs"* instead of *"children."*
18. Stresses the wrong syllable in *"photograph"* vs *"photography."*
19. Uses *"big"* five times instead of synonyms.
20. Long pause mid-sentence, then abandons the idea.
21. Produces a flawless complex sentence with inversion.
22. Listener asks to repeat three times in one answer.

### Exercise Set C — Part Identification (Questions 23–28)

Classify each question as Part 1, 2, or 3:

23. "Describe a book you read recently."
24. "Do you prefer reading paper books or e-books?"
25. "Why do some people dislike reading?"
26. "Have you ever given a book as a gift?"
27. "Should schools replace textbooks with tablets?"
28. "Describe a gift you gave someone."

### Exercise Set D — Extension Drill (Questions 29–35)

Extend each Part 1 answer to **3 sentences** (written or spoken):

29. "Do you like cooking?" → "Yes."
30. "What's the weather like where you live?" → "It's hot."
31. "Do you use public transport?" → "Sometimes."
32. "Are you good at remembering names?" → "Not really."
33. "Do you enjoy shopping?" → "No."
34. "How often do you exercise?" → "Twice a week."
35. "Do you like your neighbourhood?" → "Yes, I do."

---

## Solutions (with WHY)

### Set A

1. **Three** — standard format worldwide.
2. **One minute** — use fully for notes, not silent memorisation.
3. **One to two minutes** — under 1 minute limits FC at higher bands.
4. **Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, Pronunciation.**
5. **No** — identical Speaking test.
6. **Recording starts** — for monitoring; know this to reduce surprise.
7. **Part 2** — individual long turn.
8. **No** — unless intelligibility suffers.
9. **Brief question after Part 2** — e.g., "Would you visit again?"
10. **11–14 minutes** — varies by examiner pacing.
11. **Fluency and Coherence** — linking and flow.
12. **Yes, once** — paraphrase request allowed; not repeated help.
13. **Paper, pencil, cue card** — notes are not collected for marking.
14. **No** — one holistic band from whole interview.
15. **No direct penalty** — but offer alternative angle; silence hurts FC.

### Set B

16. **FC** — hesitation/repetition.  
17. **GRA** — morphology error.  
18. **P** — word stress.  
19. **LR** — limited range/repetition.  
20. **FC** — coherence breakdown.  
21. **GRA** — complex structure (positive).  
22. **P** (possibly FC) — intelligibility primary.

### Set C

23. **Part 2** — cue card long turn.  
24. **Part 1** — personal preference.  
25. **Part 3** — abstract/general.  
26. **Part 1** — personal experience.  
27. **Part 3** — policy/speculation.  
28. **Part 2** — cue card.

### Set D (sample extensions)

29. **Sample:** "Yes, I really enjoy cooking — especially on weekends when I'm not rushed. I usually make simple Mediterranean dishes because they use fresh ingredients and don't take too long. Last Sunday I tried a new pasta recipe I'd seen online."

**WHY 3 sentences:** Direct answer + development + specific example = Band 6+ Part 1 pattern.

---

## Review

- Speaking = **11–14 minutes**, **3 parts**, **one holistic band**.
- Four criteria **equally weighted** — weakest area caps performance.
- Part 1: extend naturally; Part 2: structure + timing; Part 3: develop and qualify.
- Recording is standard; examiner is not your enemy.
- Memorised scripts backfire; flexible strategies win.
- Integrate vocabulary and grammar from earlier book parts.

---

## Quiz

1. Duration of Part 2 preparation?
2. Which part tests sustained monologue?
3. Name two Part 1 topic areas.
4. What percentage weight does Pronunciation carry?
5. Can you use American English?
6. What follows Part 2 long turn?
7. Band 7 fluency: occasional hesitation or constant?
8. Is factual truth of stories assessed?
9. Primary fix for one-word Part 1 answers?
10. Which chapter covers pronunciation detail?

---

## Assignment

1. Record a **full mock Speaking test** (Parts 1–3) with a partner or tutor. Time each part. Score yourself 1–9 on each criterion using public descriptors.

2. Write a **personal Speaking profile** (200 words): strongest criterion, weakest criterion, top three errors, weekly plan.

3. Complete **five Part 2 cue cards** from Chapter 118 (when available) or create your own; aim for 2 minutes each. Log actual duration.

4. Watch one official IELTS Speaking sample video. Note **three examiner behaviours** (eye contact, interruptions, timing) and **three candidate strengths/weaknesses**.

---

## Revision Notes

```
SPEAKING OVERVIEW

11–14 min | 3 parts | face-to-face
P1: familiar topics, 2–4 sentences
P2: 1 min prep + 1–2 min monologue
P3: abstract discussion, 4–6 sentences
Criteria: FC | LR | GRA | P (25% each)
Weakest criterion caps band
No accent penalty if clear
Avoid memorised scripts
Record mocks; log by criterion
```

---

## Exam Tips

> **Exam Strategy:** Treat Part 1 as **real conversation** — smile, listen, answer the question asked, not a different prepared speech.

> **Exam Strategy:** In Part 2, the examiner **will** stop you at 2 minutes — hitting the full minute range is your responsibility; practise with a timer.

> **Exam Strategy:** If you misunderstand a question, ask politely: *"Could you explain what you mean by…?"* — once only.

> **Exam Strategy:** **Slow, clear speech** beats fast, mumbled speech. Fluency is not speed.

---

## Challenge Questions

1. Design a four-week Speaking plan for a candidate at Band 5.5 targeting Band 7.0, specifying daily minutes and which part receives most attention each week.

2. Explain why a candidate with excellent grammar knowledge might still score Band 6.0 in GRA under exam pressure.

3. Compare Part 3 and Writing Task 2: what skills overlap, and what skills differ because Speaking is unscripted?

---

## Band 9 Tips

> **Band 9 Secret:** Band 9 speakers **listen actively** — they reference the examiner's exact wording in Part 3 (*"You asked about whether governments should…"*) showing precise engagement.

> **Band 9 Secret:** High-band candidates treat Part 2 notes as **a map, not a script** — they glance, then speak to the examiner, not the paper.

> **Band 9 Secret:** Elite performers **self-correct lightly** (*"…or rather, what I mean is…"*) without apologising or collapsing fluency.

### Band 9 Speaking Self-Assessment Grid (original template)

| Criterion | Band 9 signal | My mock | Gap action |
|-----------|---------------|---------|------------|
| FC | Effortless flow; ideas sequenced | | |
| LR | Precise, natural, idiomatic where appropriate | | |
| GRA | Wide range; errors rare | | |
| P | Intelligible; stress/intonation enhance meaning | | |

**Discipline:** Band 9 is **consistent excellence across all four**, not one spectacular minute in Part 2.

# Chapter 115: Part 1 Strategies — Introduction & Interview

**Part:** Part 8 — Speaking

---


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Apply the **Answer–Extend–Example (AEE)** framework to any Part 1 question.
- Recognise topic clusters and predict follow-up question patterns.
- Avoid over-short and over-long answers while maintaining natural conversation rhythm.
- Use appropriate tenses, pronouns, and vocabulary for familiar personal topics.
- Handle difficult questions (unfamiliar topics, negative preferences) without freezing.
- Build a reusable Part 1 preparation bank without memorising fixed scripts.
- Self-correct and paraphrase smoothly when you make mid-answer errors.

---

## Theory / Explanation

### 115.1 The Purpose of Part 1

Part 1 lasts **4–5 minutes** and functions as a **warm-up**. The examiner asks about **familiar topics** related to your life: home, hometown, work, study, hobbies, daily routines, food, transport, weather, and similar themes.

**What Part 1 is not:**
- A formality you can ignore
- A vocabulary showcase competition
- An opportunity to recite a memorised life story

**What Part 1 is:**
- Evidence of whether you can maintain **basic fluency and coherence** under light pressure
- A sample of your **pronunciation** and **grammar in simple contexts**
- The psychological foundation for Parts 2 and 3

Candidates who treat Part 1 as "easy" and answer minimally often **enter Part 2 nervous and already scored down** on FC.

### 115.2 Question Types in Part 1

Part 1 questions fall into predictable categories:

| Type | Example | Response need |
|------|---------|---------------|
| Factual | "Where do you live?" | Clear direct fact |
| Preference | "Do you prefer tea or coffee?" | Choice + reason |
| Frequency | "How often do you exercise?" | Time expression + detail |
| Experience | "Have you ever…?" | Yes/no + narrative snippet |
| Opinion (mild) | "Do you think… is important?" | View + brief justification |
| Hypothetical (rare) | "If you could change one thing about your city…" | Conditional answer |

**Follow-up pattern:** Examiners typically ask **2–4 questions on one topic** before switching. Your first answer often determines follow-up depth.

### 115.3 The AEE Framework

The most reliable Part 1 structure is **Answer–Extend–Example**:

1. **Answer** — Respond directly in the first sentence (yes/no/what/where).
2. **Extend** — Add reason, detail, comparison, or contrast.
3. **Example** — One concrete personal instance (past or recent).

**Template (flexible, not memorised):**
> *[Direct answer]. [Reason or detail]. [For example / Actually / Last week], [specific instance].*

**Why AEE works:** It satisfies FC (development), LR (range), and GRA (compound sentences) without unnatural length. Target **20–40 seconds** per answer — roughly **2–4 sentences**.

### 115.4 Optimal Answer Length

| Length | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| 1 word | Band 4–5 signal; avoid |
| 1 sentence | Minimal; Band 5–6 unless very rich |
| 2–4 sentences | Target zone for Band 6–8 |
| 5+ sentences | Often unnatural; examiner may interrupt |

**Rule of thumb:** Stop when you have answered, extended, and exemplified. Do not wait for silence.

### 115.5 Topic Clusters and Preparation

IELTS rotates topics but themes recur. Prepare **ideas**, not scripts:

**Cluster A — Home & locality**
- Type of home, neighbourhood, favourite room, changes you'd make
- Hometown: location, size, what you like/dislike, visitors

**Cluster B — Work & study**
- Job/major, why chosen, daily tasks, future plans
- Study habits, favourite subject, school/university facilities

**Cluster C — Leisure & lifestyle**
- Hobbies, sports, reading, music, cooking, shopping
- Weekends, holidays, time with friends/family

**Cluster D — Daily life**
- Transport, sleep, meals, technology use, weather
- Morning routine, organisation, punctuality

**Preparation method:** For each cluster, prepare **3 stories** (30 seconds each) you can adapt. Example: a weekend trip story works for holidays, hobbies, and time with friends.

### 115.6 Tense and Grammar Choices

Part 1 tests basic tense control:

| Question time frame | Typical tense |
|---------------------|---------------|
| Current state | Present simple/continuous |
| Habits | Present simple + frequency adverbs |
| Past experience | Past simple; past continuous for background |
| Future plans | *going to* / *will* / present continuous for arrangements |
| Preferences | Present + *would prefer* |

**Common errors:**
- *"I am living here since 2019"* → *"I've lived here since 2019"*
- *"I am agree"* → *"I agree"*
- Switching mid-answer from past to present without signal

**Safe complex structures for Part 1:**
- *"Although I enjoy X, I don't do it as often as I'd like because…"*
- *"The main reason I prefer X is that…"*
- *"If I had more free time, I'd probably…"* (hypothetical — use accurately)

### 115.7 Lexical Resource in Part 1

You do not need obscure vocabulary. You need **precise, natural** words:

| Weak | Stronger |
|------|----------|
| good | enjoyable / convenient / refreshing |
| bad | overcrowded / unreliable / exhausting |
| like | fond of / keen on / attracted to |
| very big | spacious / vast |
| things | items / activities / aspects |

**Collocations matter:** *heavy traffic, grab a coffee, catch the bus, stuck indoors, get some fresh air.*

**Avoid:** Forcing idioms (*"hit the nail on the head"*) into every answer; misusing *"Nowadays"* as a crutch opener.

### 115.8 Handling Negative Answers

Questions about dislikes or things you don't do are **normal**:

**Question:** "Do you enjoy cooking?"  
**Honest negative:** "Not especially — I'm quite lazy in the kitchen, to be honest. I usually order delivery or eat at my parents' place on Sundays. That said, I can make a decent omelette when I have to."

**Why this works:** Direct honesty + extension + slight positive = natural, fluent answer. Never invent passion you cannot sustain in follow-ups.

### 115.9 Handling Unfamiliar Topics

If asked about something you rarely consider (e.g., singing, museums):

1. **Acknowledge honestly:** *"I don't do that very often, actually."*
2. **Redirect with related experience:** *"But I do enjoy listening to music when I commute."*
3. **Speculate lightly:** *"I suppose I'd like to try it if I had a patient teacher."*

**Do not:** Say only "I don't know" and stop.

### 115.10 Memorisation Traps

Examiners detect:
- **Scripted intros** unrelated to the question
- **Topic mismatch** (answer about "travel" when asked about "reading")
- **Flat intonation** on supposedly personal content
- **Grammar too perfect** for spontaneous speech followed by breakdown in Part 3

**Safe approach:** Memorise **structures and phrases**, not full answers. Rotate examples.

### 115.11 Interaction Skills

Part 1 is a dialogue:
- **Listen** to the full question; answer what was asked.
- **Don't interrupt** the examiner.
- **Eye contact** (cultural norms permitting) shows confidence.
- **React naturally** to surprising questions — brief *"That's an interesting question"* is acceptable once per test, not every turn.

### 115.12 Common Part 1 Errors by Band

| Band area | Typical Part 1 behaviour |
|-----------|--------------------------|
| 5 | Mostly short; repetition; limited vocabulary |
| 6 | Willing to extend but formulaic; some errors |
| 7 | Fluent with occasional hesitation; varied vocabulary |
| 8+ | Natural, flexible, precise; smooth self-correction |

---

## Examples

### Example 1: AEE Applied — Work

**Q:** "Do you work or are you a student?"  
**A:** "I'm working full-time as a junior accountant at a logistics firm."  
**E:** "I chose accounting because I was always good with numbers, and this industry is quite fast-paced, which suits me."  
**Ex:** "For instance, last month I helped reconcile shipping invoices for three warehouses — it was stressful but satisfying."

### Example 2: Preference Question

**Q:** "Do you prefer hot or cold weather?"  
**Answer:** "Definitely cold weather — I find heat draining, especially when humidity is high. In cold months I can layer up and stay active outdoors. Summer where I live gets uncomfortable; I tend to stay indoors with the air conditioning on."

### Example 3: Negative Preference

**Q:** "Do you like shopping?"  
**Answer:** "Not really — crowded malls overwhelm me, and I hate queuing. I shop online for clothes and only visit physical stores when I need to try something on, like shoes."

---

## Worked Examples

### Worked Example 1: Turning a Band 5 Answer into Band 7

**Question:** "How often do you use your phone?"

**Band 5:** "Every day. Many times."

**Revision steps:**
1. Add frequency phrase: *"Pretty much constantly throughout the day."*
2. Add reason: *"I need it for work messages and navigation."*
3. Add example/limit: *"I try to put it away after nine p.m., though, so I can sleep properly."*

**Band 7 target:** "I'd say I'm on my phone throughout the day — mainly for work emails and maps when I'm travelling between sites. I do try to disconnect after nine in the evening because otherwise I struggle to fall asleep."

### Worked Example 2: Follow-Up Chain

**Topic:** Hometown

| # | Question | Strategy |
|---|----------|----------|
| 1 | Where's your hometown? | Direct location + size |
| 2 | What do you like about it? | One like + example place |
| 3 | Has it changed much? | Compare past/present |
| 4 | Would you live there in future? | Opinion + condition |

**Planning note:** Question 3 and 4 can share the same example (new metro system) if developed differently.

### Worked Example 3: Self-Correction Without Panic

**Mid-answer error:** *"I have went to the gym…"*

**Self-correction:** *"Sorry — I **went** to the gym yesterday, actually, for a yoga class."*

**WHY:** Light self-correction shows GRA awareness; apologising repeatedly hurts FC.

## Solutions (with WHY)

### Set A (sample answers)

1. **Sample:** "I live in a rented apartment near the city centre. It's on the sixth floor, so I get quite a lot of light, which I appreciate. My favourite spot is the small balcony where I keep a few herbs."

**WHY:** Fact + detail + personal touch = natural Band 7 pattern.

2. **Sample:** "On Saturdays I usually sleep in, then meet friends for lunch. Sundays are quieter — I cook something simple and prepare for the week ahead."

### Set B

11. **Improved:** "Yes — I'm especially into jazz and lo-fi beats when I'm working. I discovered a Korean pianist on a streaming playlist last year and listen to her almost daily."

12. **Fixed:** "I've lived in Tashkent for five years." — Present perfect for duration.

13. **Fixed:** Replace repetition with reason: *"Shopping frustrates me because I dislike browsing without a clear goal."*

14. **Fixed:** "I really enjoy swimming because it's refreshing and low-impact on my knees."

15. **Expanded:** Name specifics: people, dish, atmosphere — one sentence each layer.

16. **Trimmed:** "Yes, I drink tea most mornings — usually green tea without sugar. I rarely have it in the evening because caffeine keeps me awake."

### Set C

17. **D** | 18. **B** | 19. **C** | 20. **A** | 21. **B** | 22. **C**

### Set D (strategy notes)

23. Acknowledge + related (enjoy watching) + open to trying.  
24. Acknowledge + enjoy listening + childhood stopped.  
25. Limited exposure + memorable exhibition + would visit more.  
26. Honest struggle + mobile banking helps + goal to improve.  
27. Dislike + reason (noise) + prefer quiet cafes/parks.  
28. Rarely + workplace meetings only + would like practice.

---

## Review

- Part 1 = **4–5 minutes**, familiar topics, **2–4 sentences** per answer.
- Use **AEE**: Answer, Extend, Example.
- Prepare **topic clusters**, not scripts.
- Negative/unfamiliar answers are fine if developed honestly.
- Tense accuracy and natural vocabulary beat rare words.
- Listen and answer the **actual question**.

---

## Quiz

1. What does AEE stand for?
2. Ideal sentence count for most Part 1 answers?
3. How many questions typically on one topic before switching?
4. What tense for "I've lived here since 2019"?
5. Is saying "I don't really do that" acceptable?
6. Name two topic clusters.
7. Why are one-word answers risky?
8. What is a follow-up question?
9. Should you memorise full Part 1 scripts?
10. Which part follows Part 1?

---

## Assignment

1. Record **20 Part 1 answers** (2 minutes total speaking spread across questions). Use AEE. Replay and mark FC/LR/GRA/P.

2. Build a **Part 1 idea bank**: 4 clusters × 5 bullet points of personal facts you can reuse.

3. Practise with a partner: **3 topic changes**, 4 questions each, strict timing. Partner must flag answers under 2 sentences.

4. Complete the question bank in **Chapter 116** for timed drills (10 questions daily for one week).

---

## Revision Notes

```
PART 1 STRATEGIES

4–5 min | familiar topics
AEE: Answer → Extend → Example
2–4 sentences | 20–40 sec each
Clusters: home | work/study | leisure | daily life
Honest negatives OK if developed
Structures yes, full scripts no
Self-correct once, move on
Listen → answer exact question
```

---

## Exam Tips

> **Exam Strategy:** Your **first sentence** must answer the question — examiners note directness immediately.

> **Exam Strategy:** If you use a **prepared example**, adapt it to the exact wording — mismatch is a memorisation red flag.

> **Exam Strategy:** **Don't ask** "Should I say more?" — extend naturally; the examiner will interrupt if needed.

> **Exam Strategy:** Warm up your voice **before** the test — hum, read aloud, or chat in English for 10 minutes.

---

## Challenge Questions

1. Why might a candidate who speaks English daily at work still score Band 6.0 in Part 1?

2. Design five follow-up questions an examiner might ask after "Do you enjoy cooking?" — and sketch ideal answer angles for each.

3. Compare Part 1 development strategy with Part 3 — what changes and what stays the same?

---

## Band 9 Tips

> **Band 9 Secret:** Band 9 Part 1 answers feel **effortlessly personal** — small specific details (*"a café on the corner that closes at four"*) without rehearsed polish.

> **Band 9 Secret:** High-band speakers **vary sentence openings** — not every answer begins with "Yes, I…" or "Well, I think…"

> **Band 9 Secret:** They **match register to topic** — casual tone for hobbies, slightly more formal for work/study, never stiff or academic in Part 1.

### Band 9 Model — Part 1 Mini-Set (original)

**Q:** "Do you prefer texting or calling?"  
**A:** "It depends on the situation, really. If I need a quick confirmation — like running late for dinner — I'll text. But if something's complicated or emotional, I'd rather call because tone gets lost in messages. My mother, for instance, still prefers long phone calls on Sundays, and I've got used to that ritual."

**Q:** "Has your preference changed over time?"  
**A:** "Definitely. When I was a teenager I avoided phone calls entirely; now I appreciate them more, especially for staying in touch with relatives abroad. Video calls have become part of that too — we schedule them so time zones align."

**WHY Band 9:** Natural qualification, clear examples, flexible grammar, zero strain.

## Learning Objectives

- Practise 500+ Part 1 questions across everyday topics
- Internalise a flexible answer architecture (answer → detail → example → reflect)
- Maintain fluency without sounding memorised

## Theory (quick)

Part 1 lasts 4–5 minutes. Keep answers **extended but natural** (2–4 sentences). Avoid one-word replies and avoid Task 2 lectures.

## Question Bank with Band 9 Models


### Topic: Hometown
#### Q1. Do you like hometown?

**Band 9 model answer**  
Well, regarding hometown, I’d say it depends on the day, but generally I try to be intentional about it. For example, I usually approach it in a practical way: I notice what actually improves my routine rather than what looks impressive. That said, I’m not rigid — if circumstances change, I’m happy to adapt. Overall, it’s something I value because it quietly shapes how productive and balanced I feel.

**Why this scores high:** direct answer → personalised detail → concession → reflective close; natural discourse markers; no memorised essay tone.

That said, I’m not rigid — if circumstances change, I’m happy to adapt. Overall, it’s something I value because it quietly shapes how productive and balanced I feel.

**Why this scores high:** direct answer → personalised detail → concession → reflective close; natural discourse markers; no memorised essay tone.

## Review

Rotate topics weekly. Record answers and track filler words (*erm*, *like*).

## Assignment

Answer 40 questions timed (20 seconds thinking max each). Transcribe five weakest answers and upgrade vocabulary/grammar.

## Exam Tips

Smile with your voice; paraphrase the question lightly; self-correct once if needed, then move on.

# Chapter 117: Part 2 Strategies — The Long Turn

**Part:** Part 8 — Speaking

---


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Use the **one-minute preparation time** efficiently to build a speakable note map.
- Structure a **1–2 minute monologue** that addresses all cue card bullet points without sounding read aloud.
- Apply flexible narrative frameworks (PPF, STAR, timeline) to diverse cue card topics.
- Manage timing so you speak for at least **90 seconds** and up to 2 minutes confidently.
- Handle abstract or unfamiliar cue cards by adapting prepared story skeletons.
- Maintain fluency when you lose your place or forget a planned detail.
- Respond appropriately to Part 2 rounding-off questions.

---

## Theory / Explanation

### 117.1 The Purpose of Part 2

Part 2 is the **individual long turn**. You receive a cue card, prepare for **1 minute**, then speak for **1–2 minutes** without interruption from the examiner (except to signal time).

**What Part 2 tests:**
- Ability to **speak at length** on your own
- **Organisation** and coherence of extended speech
- Range of **vocabulary and grammar** in monologue mode
- **Pronunciation** sustained over time

Part 2 often produces the **clearest band signal** because the examiner hears uninterrupted production. Weak Part 2 performance is difficult to recover from in Part 3.

### 117.2 Cue Card Anatomy

Typical format:

```
Describe [person/place/event/object/experience/skill/etc.]
You should say:
- [bullet 1 — usually what/who]
- [bullet 2 — when/where/how]
- [bullet 3 — detail or relationship]
and explain [bullet 4 — why/feeling/significance]
```

**Optional line:** *"You will have one minute to prepare… You have one to two minutes to speak. Don't worry if I stop you…"*

**Critical rule:** Address **all bullets**. Missing one bullet caps Task achievement equivalent in FC — the examiner notices gaps.

### 117.3 The One-Minute Preparation Protocol

**Seconds 0–10:** Read entire card twice. Underline **topic** and **explain** line.

**Seconds 10–40:** Write **note map** (not sentences):
- Keywords only
- One word triggers memory
- Arrows for sequence

**Seconds 40–55:** Mentally rehearse **opening sentence** and **closing sentence**.

**Seconds 55–60:** Look up; breathe; begin when examiner indicates.

**What not to do during prep:**
- Write full sentences (wastes time)
- Memorise an essay silently (causes robotic delivery)
- Panic if topic is unfamiliar (adapt a story skeleton)

### 117.4 Note-Mapping Templates

**Timeline map** (events, trips, life changes):
```
Past → Event → Detail → Present impact
2019 | Kyoto | temples | still recommend
```

**PPF map** (Past–Present–Future) — works for habits, places, people:
```
Past: child — grandma's kitchen
Present: cook weekly — pasta
Future: teach niece
```

**STAR map** (Situation–Task–Action–Result) — skills, achievements:
```
S: office slow reports
T: learn Excel macros
A: online course 3 months
R: saved 5 hrs/week
```

**Sensory map** (places, objects):
```
See: golden roof
Hear: busy market
Feel: humid air
Meaning: first solo trip
```

### 117.5 Monologue Structure Frameworks

**Framework A — Classic narrative (4 blocks)**

1. **Introduction (15–20 sec):** State topic; set scene.
2. **Body 1 (25–30 sec):** First bullet + vivid detail.
3. **Body 2 (25–30 sec):** Second/third bullets woven together.
4. **Conclusion (15–20 sec):** "Explain" bullet — feelings, significance, recommendation.

**Framework B — Topic sentence per bullet**

Each bullet becomes one **mini-paragraph** of 2–3 sentences. Simple and reliable for Band 6–7.

**Framework C — Thematic depth**

Choose **one theme** (e.g., "learning independence") and thread all bullets through it. Stronger for Band 8+ if controlled.

### 117.6 Opening and Closing Sentences

**Strong openings (adapt, don't memorise one):**
- *"I'd like to talk about…"*
- *"The [person/place] I'd like to describe is…"*
- *"Something that comes to mind is…"*

**Strong closings:**
- *"So overall, that's why this experience stayed with me."*
- *"Looking back, I'd definitely recommend it because…"*
- *"That's the main reason it mattered so much to me."*

**Avoid:** *"That's all I can say"* (signals inability to extend).

### 117.7 Timing Management

| Duration | Assessment signal |
|----------|-------------------|
| Under 1 min | Insufficient FC for Band 7+ |
| 1:00–1:30 | Adequate minimum |
| 1:30–2:00 | Strong target |
| Forced stop at 2:00 | Good — examiner had more to listen to |

**Practice method:** Record 10 cue cards; log duration. If under 1:30, add **sensory detail** or **comparison** (*"Unlike other cities I've visited…"*).

### 117.8 Vocabulary and Grammar for Part 2

Part 2 invites **descriptive language**:

| Function | Language |
|----------|----------|
| Setting scene | *"It was a chilly autumn morning when…"*
| Emphasis | *"What struck me most was…"*
| Feelings | *"I felt overwhelmed / relieved / proud"*
| Comparison | *"Compared with my expectations…"*
| Reason | *"The main reason I chose it was…"*

**Grammar range:**
- Past narrative: past simple + past continuous + past perfect (one instance)
- Relative clauses: *"The friend who recommended it…"*
- Participle clauses: *"Having never tried it before, I was nervous."*

**Balance:** Two complex structures well-used beat five broken ones.

### 117.9 When the Topic Is Unfamiliar

**Strategy 1 — Closest true story:** Cue card asks about a museum you haven't visited → describe a **gallery or historical site** you have.

**Strategy 2 — Hypothetical frame (careful):** *"I haven't done this often, but one experience that fits is…"*

**Strategy 3 — Person/object pivot:** *"Describe a law"* → talk about a **rule at school/work** that affected you (if genuinely relevant).

**Never:** Invent an implausible celebrity-dinner story; follow-ups in Part 3 may expose inconsistency.

### 117.10 Delivery: Notes vs Eye Contact

- Glance at notes **briefly**; speak to examiner.
- Notes are **triggers**, not a script to read.
- If you lose place, pause, look at notes, resume: *"Where was I — ah yes, the second point…"*

### 117.11 Rounding-Off Questions

After Part 2, examiner asks **1–2 short questions** requiring brief answers:

- *"Would you like to do that again?"*
- *"Do your friends enjoy that too?"*

**Answer in 1–2 sentences.** Do not restart a new monologue.

### 117.12 Common Part 2 Failure Patterns

| Error | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| Stops at 45 seconds | Pre-plan closing; add example |
| Reads notes word-for-word | Keyword notes only |
| Ignores a bullet | Check off bullets while practising |
| Lists without linking | Use sequencers: *"After that… Later…"*
| Flat tone | Vary stress; pause before key points |
| Wrong tense throughout | Mark tense on notes (P/S/F) |

### 117.13 Cue Card Topic Categories

Although every cue card is unique, most fit **recurring categories**. Recognising the category during your 1-minute prep helps you choose the right framework instantly.

| Category | Typical verbs | Best framework | Example topics |
|----------|---------------|----------------|----------------|
| Person | describe someone, a teacher, a friend | PPF or character arc | influential person, family member, famous person |
| Place | describe a city, building, quiet place | Sensory + timeline | hometown, café, museum, natural site |
| Event | describe a celebration, accident, achievement | Timeline narrative | wedding, festival, sports event |
| Object | describe a gift, book, photo, device | Description + significance | phone, photograph, traditional product |
| Activity | describe a hobby, sport, skill | STAR or PPF | cooking skill, language learned, project |
| Experience | describe a trip, meal, challenge | Timeline + reflection | journey, difficult decision, proud moment |
| Abstract | describe a law, tradition, goal | Thematic + example | important rule, future ambition, tradition |

**Cross-category adaptation:** A "person" story can answer an "event" card if the event centred on that person. A "place" story can answer "experience" if you frame it as *"an experience that took place in…"*

### 117.14 The 90-Second Safety Net

If you tend to finish early, pre-load a **safety net layer** you add only when time remains:

1. **Comparison:** *"Compared with other places I've visited…"*
2. **Sensory detail:** one sound, smell, or texture
3. **Emotional reflection:** *"Looking back, I realise…"*
4. **Recommendation:** *"I'd suggest going in… / avoiding…"*
5. **Future link:** *"I'd like to return / I'd never repeat…"*

Practise delivering the core story in 75 seconds, then attach one safety-net layer to reach 95 seconds. In the exam, if you hit 1:45 naturally, skip the safety net — do not pad mechanically.

### 117.15 Part 2 and Part 3 Handoff

Part 2 content **feeds** Part 3 but should not **repeat** it. During prep, note one **general theme** from your story (e.g., solo travel → independence; coding skill → lifelong learning). When Part 3 opens, shift register from personal narrative to societal analysis. Mentally "close" Part 2 with a clean ending so Part 3 feels like a new conversation, not an extension of the monologue.

---

## Examples

### Example 1: Note Map

**Cue card:** Describe a place you visited on holiday.

```
Place: coastal town — Essaouira, Morocco
When: 2022, spring, 4 days
Who: solo + met photographer
Why impressed: medina, wind, seafood, calm pace
Recommend: yes — artists, not party town
```

### Example 2: Opening + Body Extract

*"I'd like to talk about Essaouira, a coastal town in Morocco I visited in spring 2022. I went alone for four days — my first proper solo trip — and I'd seen photos of the old medina walls against the Atlantic, so I was curious. What impressed me most was the contrast between the busy blue-and-white alleys inside the walls and the wide, windy beach outside, where kite surfers gather every afternoon."*

### Example 3: Closing Extract

*"So overall, it left me with this sense of calm I don't usually get on holiday. I'd recommend it to anyone who wants culture and sea air without the intensity of bigger tourist cities — though I'd suggest going in spring before the summer crowds arrive."*

---

## Worked Examples

### Worked Example 1: Bullet Coverage Check

**Cue card bullets vs speech plan:**

| Bullet | Covered? | Speech segment |
|--------|----------|----------------|
| what place | ✓ | Opening sentence |
| when you went | ✓ | Body 1 |
| who with | ✓ | Body 1 |
| why impressed | ✓ | Body 2 |
| explain recommend | ✓ | Closing |

**Self-check habit:** Tick bullets on cue card during practice.

### Worked Example 2: Extending from 1:05 to 1:45

**Original stop point:** Finished story after main event.

**Additions:**
- Sensory detail (+15 sec): sounds, smells, weather
- Comparison (+10 sec): *"Unlike package tours I've done…"*
- Reflection (+15 sec): what you learned / how you changed

### Worked Example 3: Recovery After Freeze

**Situation:** Forgot friend's name at 1:00 mark.

**Recovery:** *"My friend — I'm blanking on her surname, but we were at university together — suggested we try this restaurant. Anyway, the food was…"*

**WHY:** Brief honest recovery beats long silent panic.

---

## Practice Exercises

### Exercise Set A — Note Mapping (Questions 1–5)

Create **keyword note maps** (prep time: 1 minute each):

1. Describe a person who has influenced you.
2. Describe a piece of technology you find useful.
3. Describe a time you helped someone.
4. Describe a goal you want to achieve in the future.
5. Describe a traditional product from your country.

### Exercise Set B — Structure Labelling (Questions 6–10)

For a 2-minute speech on "a skill you learned," label times for:
6. Introduction  
7. How learned  
8. Who helped  
9. Why useful  
10. Closing recommendation  

### Exercise Set C — Problem Fixing (Questions 11–15)

Identify the problem and fix:

11. Candidate speaks 50 seconds; stops smiling; silence.
12. Notes contain 120 words of full sentences.
13. Candidate never mentions "when" despite bullet on card.
14. Candidate reads notes without looking up for 2 minutes.
15. Opening: *"I will tell you about many things about my holiday."*

### Exercise Set D — Framework Selection (Questions 16–20)

Choose best framework (Timeline / PPF / STAR / Sensory):

16. Describe a life-changing event.  
17. Describe your favourite room.  
18. Describe a work project you completed.  
19. Describe a habit you want to change.  
20. Describe a memorable meal.  

---

## Solutions (with WHY)

### Set A (sample map — Question 1)

```
Person: aunt — lawyer — ethical, calm
Influence: teenage — parents divorced
How: modelled resilience, study habits
Now: call before big decisions
```

### Set B (sample timing)

6. 0:00–0:20 | 7. 0:20–0:55 | 8. 0:55–1:20 | 9. 1:20–1:45 | 10. 1:45–2:00

### Set C

11. **Under-length** — add reflection + recommendation.  
12. **Over-writing** — keywords only.  
13. **Bullet gap** — insert time phrase early.  
14. **Delivery** — practise glancing.  
15. **Vague opening** — name specific holiday destination immediately.

### Set D

16. Timeline | 17. Sensory | 18. STAR | 19. PPF | 20. Sensory + Timeline

---

## Review

- Part 2 = **1 min prep + 1–2 min speak**.
- Notes = **keywords**, not scripts.
- Cover **every bullet** explicitly.
- Target **90+ seconds**; aim for natural stop at 2:00.
- Use frameworks: narrative, PPF, STAR, sensory.
- Rounding-off = **short** answers.
- Practise with timer and recording.

---

## Quiz

1. How long is Part 2 preparation?
2. Minimum speak duration for Band 7 ambition?
3. What should notes contain?
4. Name two monologue frameworks.
5. What happens at 2 minutes?
6. How many rounding-off questions typically?
7. Should you invent stories?
8. What is PPF?
9. Best opening strategy?
10. Which chapter has cue card practice bank?

---

## Assignment

1. Complete **8 cue cards** from Chapter 118 (or create your own). Record each; log duration and bullet coverage.

2. Practise **1-minute prep only** — no speaking — for 10 cards daily for 3 days. Review note quality.

3. Deliver one speech **without notes** after prep — tests internalisation.

4. Write a **personal story skeleton library**: 5 stories adaptable to 15+ cue card types.

---

## Revision Notes

```
PART 2 STRATEGIES

1 min prep | 1–2 min speak
Notes: keywords, maps, arrows
Frameworks: timeline | PPF | STAR | sensory
Open: state topic clearly
Close: explain bullet + recommend/reflect
90 sec minimum | 2 min ideal
Glance notes; speak to examiner
Rounding-off: 1–2 sentences
All bullets mandatory
```

---

## Exam Tips

> **Exam Strategy:** The **"explain" line** on the cue card is your closing — plan it during prep even if you speak it last.

> **Exam Strategy:** If the examiner **stops you**, that's often positive — you filled the time.

> **Exam Strategy:** Put **tense markers** on notes: P / Pr / F — prevents mid-story tense chaos.

> **Exam Strategy:** Breathe at bullet **transitions** — micro-pauses sound natural, not hesitant.

---

## Challenge Questions

1. Why do examiners prefer keyword notes to full sentences? Link to FC and P criteria.

2. Map 10 diverse cue card topics to **5 reusable story skeletons** — show how adaptation works.

3. Compare Part 2 monologue coherence with Writing Task 1 report structure — what organisational skills overlap?

---

## Band 9 Tips

> **Band 9 Secret:** Band 9 Part 2 speeches **sound discovered, not delivered** — the candidate appears to relive the experience with selective vivid detail.

> **Band 9 Secret:** They use **one well-chosen anecdote** rather than listing ten facts.

> **Band 9 Secret:** Discourse markers are **invisible** — no mechanical *"Firstly… Secondly…"* unless topic truly requires sequence.

### Band 9 Model — Part 2 Extract (original cue card: Describe a quiet place)

*"I'd like to describe a small public library branch about ten minutes from my apartment — not the main city library, but a converted house on a residential street. I stumbled on it during the pandemic when cafés were closed and I couldn't focus at home. What makes it quiet isn't silence — you sometimes hear pages or a kettle in the staff room — but the sense that nobody expects anything of you. The reading room has these low wooden desks by a window overlooking a garden, and in winter the radiator ticks, which oddly helps me concentrate. I still go there when I need to think through a difficult email or read without my phone. I'd recommend it to anyone who finds open-plan offices or noisy co-working spaces draining — though I'd mention it closes early on Sundays, so timing matters."*

**Duration:** ~1:50 | **Bullets:** all covered | **Features:** sensory detail, reflection, qualified recommendation.

---

## Learning Objectives

## Strategy reminder

1. Underline task words  
2. Note 5–7 bullets (not sentences)  
3. Speak in chronological or importance order  
4. End with reflection / future comment  

## Cue Card Bank

### Cue Card 1: Describe a person who influenced you in your country

You should say:
- who
- how you met
- what they did
- why influential
and explain why this is worth talking about.

**1-minute notes:** Who/what → setting → 2 details → feeling/result → future comment

**Useful vocabulary:** memorable, influential, atmosphere, gradually, unexpectedly, worthwhile, perspective

**Band 9 sample (approx. 2 minutes):**  
I’d like to talk about a person who influenced you in your country. To begin with, it stands out because it reshaped how I see everyday choices. I first became aware of it in a fairly ordinary situation, but the details stayed with me. What made it significant was not only what happened, but how people responded — patiently, thoughtfully, and with clear priorities. Looking back, I realise it strengthened my ability to evaluate options under pressure. If a similar situation arose again, I would handle it with more confidence and clearer communication.

**Examiner note:** Clear staging, specific yet flexible detail, controlled complex sentences, natural ending.

# Chapter 119: Part 3 Strategies — Two-Way Discussion

**Part:** Part 8 — Speaking

---


<div class="chapter-meta">

| | |
|---|---|
| **Estimated study time** | 45–120 minutes (adjust by level) |
| **Prerequisites** | Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked |
| **Difficulty** | Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks |
| **Key takeaways** | Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing |

</div>

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Recognise Part 3 question types (opinion, compare, cause/effect, speculate, evaluate).
- Apply the **OEE** framework (Opinion–Explain–Example) and **balanced view** patterns.
- Develop abstract answers in **4–6 sentences** without lecturing or drifting off-topic.
- Handle examiner challenges and rephrased questions calmly.
- Use hedging, qualification, and contrast appropriate to academic discussion.
- Connect Part 3 themes to Part 2 without repeating the same story verbatim.
- Demonstrate grammatical range (conditionals, comparatives, modal verbs) under pressure.

---

## Theory / Explanation

### 119.1 The Purpose of Part 3

Part 3 lasts **4–5 minutes** and is a **two-way discussion** linked to the Part 2 theme. Questions move from **personal** to **general**, **abstract**, and **analytical**.

**Example progression (Part 2: a useful skill):**
- Part 3: *"What skills are important for children today?"*
- Then: *"Should schools focus more on practical skills?"*
- Then: *"How might automation change the job market?"*

**What Part 3 tests:**
- Ability to **analyse**, not only describe
- **Fluency** under conceptual pressure
- **Lexical resource** for abstract topics (society, technology, education, environment)
- **Grammar range** — conditionals, passive, complex noun phrases

Part 3 separates **Band 6.5** from **Band 7.5+** more often than Part 1.

### 119.2 Question Type Taxonomy

| Type | Signal words | Response strategy |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| Opinion | "Do you think…?" | Clear view + reasons |
| Compare | "Compare… / differences…" | Both sides + contrast language |
| Cause/effect | "Why…? / What causes…?" | 2–3 factors + example |
| Speculation | "How might… in future?" | Modal verbs + cautious claims |
| Evaluate | "Is it positive or negative?" | Balanced view + judgement |
| Hypothetical | "If… what would…?" | Second conditional accurately |
| Generalisation | "Why do people…?" | Avoid over-generalising; hedge |

### 119.3 The OEE Framework

**Opinion–Explain–Example** — Part 3's core structure:

1. **Opinion** — Direct answer in sentence 1.
2. **Explain** — Reasons, mechanisms, comparison.
3. **Example** — Society-level or personal illustration.

**Extended OEE+ (Band 7.5+):**
4. **Qualify** — *"That said… / On the other hand…"*
5. **Mini-conclusion** — *"So overall…"*

**Target length:** **4–6 sentences**, **40–60 seconds**. Longer answers risk examiner interruption — not always bad, but can signal lack of focus.

### 119.4 Balanced and Two-Part Answers

Many Part 3 questions invite **balance**:

**Question:** "Is tourism always beneficial for local communities?"

**Structure:**
- Sentence 1: *"Not always — it depends on how it's managed."*
- Sentences 2–3: Benefits (jobs, infrastructure)
- Sentences 4–5: Drawbacks (overcrowding, price inflation)
- Sentence 6: Judgement (*"On balance, regulated tourism helps if…"*)

**Why balance works:** Shows LR (contrast lexis) and FC (logical sequencing) without needing "correct" policy expertise.

### 119.5 Hedging and Qualification

Native-like academic speech **hedges** claims:

| Too absolute | Hedged |
|--------------|--------|
| "All teenagers use phones." | "Many teenagers seem to rely on phones." |
| "Technology ruins education." | "Technology can distract students if unused thoughtfully." |
| "Governments must ban cars." | "Governments could incentivise public transport instead." |

**Useful phrases:**
- *"It tends to… / It's often argued that…"*
- *"From what I've observed… / In many cases…"*
- *"I'm not an expert, but…"* (once only — don't undermine every answer)

### 119.6 Grammar Range for Part 3

**High-value structures:**

| Structure | Example fragment |
|-----------|------------------|
| Second conditional | *"If cities invested more in cycling, congestion might ease."* |
| Third conditional | *"If governments had acted earlier, emissions could have fallen."* |
| Passive | *"Children are often exposed to advertising online."* |
| Relative clauses | *"Policies that prioritise renewable energy…"*
| Concession | *"Although online learning is flexible, it lacks face-to-face interaction."* |
| Comparative | *"The more accessible education becomes, the more competitive the job market may get."* |

**Rule:** One or two complex structures **per answer**, used accurately.

### 119.7 Lexical Resource for Abstract Topics

Part 3 rewards **topic vocabulary** from Part 3 of this book (Chapters 45–70):

| Topic | Sample lexis |
|-------|--------------|
| Education | curriculum, literacy, vocational training, rote learning |
| Technology | automation, digital divide, privacy, algorithms |
| Environment | carbon footprint, sustainable, emissions, conservation |
| Society | demographic, inequality, urbanisation, social cohesion |
| Work | gig economy, job security, upskilling, remote work |

**Paraphrase the question** to show range: *"Why do people move to cities?"* → *"urban migration / seek better prospects / rural decline"*

### 119.8 Handling Examiner Prompts

Examiners may:
- **Rephrase** if you misunderstand
- **Ask "Why?"** to probe depth
- **Interrupt** to move on — normal, not a failure signal
- **Challenge**: *"But some people would disagree — why?"*

**Responses:**
- Welcome probes: *"That's a fair point — I think the reason is…"*
- Don't restart from zero; **extend** previous idea
- If lost: *"Could I think about that for a moment?"* — brief pause OK

### 119.9 Connecting to Part 2 Without Repeating

You **may** reference Part 2 briefly:
- *"Like the skill I mentioned earlier, communication matters in teams too."*

**Avoid:**
- Retelling entire Part 2 story
- Forcing irrelevant personal anecdotes into abstract questions

**Ratio:** ~70% general/societal, ~30% personal illustration in Part 3.

### 119.10 Common Part 3 Failure Patterns

| Pattern | Problem | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| Essay mode | 2-minute monologue | OEE; stop at 6 sentences |
| Echoing question | Repeats examiner words only | Paraphrase then answer |
| No position | "It depends" without development | Depends **because** X and Y |
| Memorised statistics | Sounds fake | Use plausible examples |
| Part 1 register | Too casual for abstract topic | Slightly more formal lexis |
| Panic vocabulary | Long pauses | Simplify; paraphrase |

### 119.11 Part 3 vs Writing Task 2

| Skill | Writing Task 2 | Part 3 |
|-------|----------------|--------|
| Idea development | Paragraphs | 4–6 sentences |
| Planning time | 5 minutes | ~2 seconds |
| Evidence | Examples required | Examples helpful |
| Cohesion | Paragraph linking | Spoken markers |
| Revision | Can edit | Self-correct only |

**Transfer:** If you can outline Task 2 essays, you already have Part 3 **ideas** — practise **oral compression**.

### 119.12 Topic Preparation Strategy

Prepare **idea clusters**, not answers:

For each common theme, prepare:
- 2 advantages, 2 disadvantages
- 1 cause, 1 effect
- 1 future prediction
- 1 personal mini-example

**Themes:** education, work, technology, environment, media, health, transport, culture, family, cities.

---

## Examples

### Example 1: Opinion Question

**Q:** "Do you think children should learn a foreign language at primary school?"

**OEE answer:** "Yes — I think starting early is generally beneficial because young children pick up pronunciation more naturally. Schools can integrate languages through songs and games rather than heavy grammar. For example, in my country some primary schools introduce English twice a week, and pupils seem less self-conscious than teenagers. That said, it shouldn't crowd out the mother tongue — balance matters."

### Example 2: Speculation Question

**Q:** "How might cities change in the next twenty years?"

**Answer:** "I imagine they'll become more compact and public-transport oriented, partly because of climate targets. We might see fewer private cars in centres, with more cycling infrastructure and electric buses. At the same time, remote work could reduce rush-hour pressure, though housing affordability will remain a challenge. It's hard to predict exactly, but sustainability will probably drive most planning decisions."

### Example 3: Examiner Challenge

**Q:** "But isn't tourism harmful to the environment?"  
**Response:** "Absolutely — it can be, especially when visitors fly long distances for short trips. That's why many destinations now promote longer stays and off-season travel to spread impact. The harm isn't inevitable; it depends on policy and tourist behaviour."

---

## Worked Examples

### Worked Example 1: Band 6 → Band 7 Upgrade

**Q:** "Why do some people dislike reading?"

**Band 6:** "Because reading is boring and they prefer phones. Phones have videos. Reading takes time."

**Band 7 revision:**
- Merge choppy sentences
- Add hedge + second reason
- Include societal example

**Target:** "I think it's often a habit issue — people are used to fast digital content, so books feel slow by comparison. There's also a confidence factor; if someone struggled with reading at school, they may avoid it as an adult. In many countries libraries try to address this with community programmes, but screen time keeps rising."

### Worked Example 2: Two-Part Question

**Q:** "What problems do fast-growing cities face, and how can governments respond?"

**Plan (mental 5 sec):**
- Problems: housing, transport, pollution
- Responses: planning, investment, regulation

**Answer structure:** Problem 1 + Problem 2 + Response 1 + Response 2 + brief balance.

### Worked Example 3: Conditional Accuracy

**Q:** "If you could change one thing about education in your country, what would it be?"

**Weak:** *"If I will change, I change teacher pay."*

**Strong:** *"If I could change one thing, I'd raise teacher training standards rather than only salaries — better-trained teachers tend to improve outcomes across subjects. I'd model it on countries where mentoring is mandatory in the first two years."*

## Solutions (with WHY)

### Set A

1. Compare/Opinion | 2. Speculate/Opinion | 3. Cause | 4. Hypothetical | 5. Evaluate  
6. Compare/Cause | 7. Opinion | 8. Cause | 9. Speculate | 10. Compare

### Set B (sample — Question 11)

"Personally, I'd limit homework rather than ban it entirely — young children need downtime and play. Too many assignments can create stress for families, especially when parents work long hours. Short tasks that reinforce reading or basic maths seem reasonable. For instance, ten minutes of reading aloud might work better than worksheets. The key is quality and age-appropriate expectations, not volume."

### Set C (sample — Question 17)

Acknowledge economic benefits; mention crowding and resident displacement; suggest caps or ticketing; conclude with balanced tourism management.

### Set D (grammar checks)

21. *"If cities built more cycle lanes, more commuters might leave their cars at home."*  
22. *"Students are assessed through standardised tests in many systems."*  
23. *"Although tablets can engage pupils, they can also distract without clear rules."*

---

## Review

- Part 3 = **abstract discussion**, 4–5 minutes, linked to Part 2 theme.
- Use **OEE** (+ qualify for higher bands).
- **4–6 sentences** per answer; avoid essay mode.
- Hedge generalisations; use topic vocabulary accurately.
- Conditionals, concession, passive — **one per answer** if accurate.
- Interruptions and **Why?** probes are normal — extend, don't panic.

---

## Quiz

1. How long is Part 3 approximately?
2. What does OEE stand for?
3. Ideal sentence count per answer?
4. Name two Part 3 question types.
5. Should Part 3 answers be mostly personal stories?
6. What is hedging?
7. How to handle "Why?" follow-up?
8. One grammar structure valuable in Part 3?
9. Connection between Part 2 and Part 3 themes?
10. Which book part provides topic lexis?

---

## Assignment

1. Record **15 Part 3 answers** (5 minutes) from Chapter 120 question bank or create your own. Apply OEE.

2. Take **3 Writing Task 2 questions**; outline essay in 5 minutes; deliver **oral Part 3-style answer** in 60 seconds each.

3. Practise **examiner role-play**: partner asks main question + 2 follow-ups per topic.

4. Build **theme sheets** for 5 topics: 4 bullet ideas + 5 key words each.

---

## Revision Notes

```
PART 3 STRATEGIES

4–5 min | abstract | linked to Part 2
OEE: Opinion → Explain → Example
4–6 sentences | hedge claims
Balance: both sides + judgement
Grammar: conditional, passive, concession
70% general / 30% personal
Welcome Why? probes
Don't repeat Part 2 monologue
Topic lexis from Part 3 vocab chapters
```

---

## Exam Tips

> **Exam Strategy:** **Answer first sentence** — don't build suspense; examiners assess clarity early.

> **Exam Strategy:** If you need thinking time, use a **short filler**: *"That's an interesting question — I'd say…"* — not repeated every turn.

> **Exam Strategy:** **Paraphrase** the question in your opening to show LR: *"Why people migrate to cities… I'd point to economic opportunity first."*

> **Exam Strategy:** End gracefully when you've developed — **don't wait** for the examiner to cut you off every time.

---

## Challenge Questions

1. Why can a strong Part 2 followed by weak Part 3 produce Band 6.5 overall rather than Band 7?

2. Design a Part 3 question ladder (5 questions) for the Part 2 topic "Describe an important tradition in your country."

3. Compare hedging in Speaking Part 3 with cautious academic writing — same or different?

---

## Band 9 Tips

> **Band 9 Secret:** Band 9 candidates **anticipate the angle** of the next question — their Part 3 answers naturally set up follow-ups without scripting.

> **Band 9 Secret:** They use **precise collocation** (*"ease congestion," "bridge the digital divide"*) without sounding like a textbook.

> **Band 9 Secret:** When challenged, they **concede partial truth** then refine their position — hallmark of sophisticated discussion.

### Band 9 Model — Part 3 Mini-Set (original; theme: skills/learning)

**Q:** "What skills should schools prioritise today?"  
**A:** "I'd prioritise critical thinking and digital literacy alongside literacy and numeracy — not instead of them. Students need to evaluate online information because so much learning happens on screens now. Collaboration matters too, since many workplaces are project-based. That said, schools shouldn't neglect practical life skills like financial basics, which parents sometimes assume children will pick up naturally."

**Q:** "Has the internet made traditional teachers less important?"  
**A:** "Not really — it's changed their role. Teachers act more as guides who structure discussion rather than sole sources of facts, because facts are searchable. The human element — motivation, feedback, pastoral care — is still hard to automate. Where internet access is uneven, though, relying on online resources can widen inequality, so policy has to catch up."

**WHY Band 9:** Clear positions, balanced qualification, abstract vocabulary, natural fluency, no memorisation smell.

## Learning Objectives

- Handle abstract discussion with flexible argumentation

## Theory

Part 3 rewards: extended turns, speculation, comparison, evaluation, and precise vocabulary — without sounding like a memorised essay.

## Question Bank


### Theme: Education systems
#### Q1. Why do you think education systems has become more important recently?

**Band 9 model:** That’s a layered question. On the one hand, education systems clearly intersects with economic incentives and social norms, so simple answers rarely work. On the other hand, we do have practical levers — policy design, education, and transparent information — that can shift behaviour over time. A balanced view is that progress is possible, but only if short-term convenience is weighed against long-term costs. Personally, I would prioritise measures that are fair, evidence-based, and easy for ordinary people to follow.

**Examiner feedback:** Addresses complexity, offers positions with support, uses discourse management, avoids absolute claims.
